The Orbit of Zayn al-Abidin

They say that when Zayn al-Abidin, Ali ibn al-Husayn, made the pilgrimage from Medina and returned, he would not remove his mount’s saddle. The round trip was close to a thousand kilometres.

Why? Because this animal had been his companion. She had carried the burden of taking him to the House of God and bringing him home again. She, too, was a living spirit, and a living spirit was not to be insulted or harmed.

And what would he do if she suddenly refused to move somewhere along the road? He would simply go along with her. If she stopped, he stopped. He would wait until her mood improved, and then they would continue.

But kindness to animals does not necessarily prove that someone is humane. Plenty of Westerners treat animals gently and pamper them, while in every other respect behaving like predators toward other human beings—especially toward people of another colour.

That was not Zayn al-Abidin.

Another story tells us that one of his slaves was roasting meat in an oven while a young son of Zayn al-Abidin stood nearby. The skewer slipped from the slave’s hand, struck the child on the head, and killed him.

Zayn al-Abidin heard the cry and rushed over. When he saw his son covered in blood, he did not turn to him first. He turned to the slave and said:

“Don’t be afraid. Don’t be afraid. You are free. You are free.”

Only then did he turn to his son. The child was already dead. He picked him up and covered him.

For Zayn al-Abidin, the urgent problem at that moment was the slave, who was almost dying of terror at what had happened. Zayn al-Abidin understood this and dealt with the man’s fear before attending to his own son. To make him feel completely safe, he freed him on the spot.

Slaves were normally freed as a reward for some great service. They were not freed because they had accidentally—or deliberately—killed their master’s child.

Zayn al-Abidin was a believing Muslim, deeply committed to doctrine and religious law. One sign of that commitment was that he owned slaves, because slavery was legally permitted. He saw no defect in the law so long as it came from God.

But Zayn al-Abidin’s ethics rose above his beliefs.

His conduct shows the role ethics can play in softening the cruelty of law. He gives us an example of something every legal system needs: moral principles capable of tempering its rigidity and strict literalism.

I had been looking for a title for this Orbit on Sufi ethics, and I chose Zayn al-Abidin.

I could just as well have chosen Plekhanov, the Russian Marxist philosopher.

What made me think of him was something he wrote in the introduction to his book The Monist View of History, which contained his debates with a Russian bourgeois thinker named Mikhailovsky. Plekhanov said that further ideas and replies had occurred to him after the original exchange, but he refused to add them to the book because Mikhailovsky had died. It would not be right, he said, to add new arguments to replies written while Mikhailovsky was alive, since the man would no longer be able to read them or answer them.

That is the same ethic we see in Zayn al-Abidin.

I chose Zayn al-Abidin simply because he came earlier.

Plekhanov has another standing of his own, one that Zayn al-Abidin does not share outside questions of ethics, and his proper place is elsewhere in this book.

I had wanted to include him among my list of God’s cherished ones, but some friends suggested that, among the Russians, I should limit myself to Plekhanov and Tolstoy, since between them they could stand for the others of their kind. I accepted their advice, while keeping my affection for him.

Ethics

Khuluq—moral character—is a quality in a person. It may be stable or changing, innate or acquired.

In Arabic the word is pronounced khuluq, though the middle consonant can also be left unstressed. Popular speech later produced from it the meaning of mood or psychological state. Iraqis say, “My khuluq has narrowed,” meaning that they feel distressed or upset. People in the Levant may say, “Let me ease my khuluq,” meaning: let me relieve this inner pressure.

But ordinary people also use the original moral sense.

The positive meaning predominates. Shawqi writes:

Nations endure only as long as their morals endure; when their morals disappear, they disappear as well.

Ordinary people say, “So-and-so has no morals.”

Educated people say instead that someone has “bad morals” or “high morals.”

It is better to preserve the positive sense as the word’s primary meaning. For the opposite we can say: bad traits and noble traits, bad conduct and good conduct.

Arabic has several near-synonyms.

Shamāʾil usually refers to good qualities.

Sajaya means deeply rooted traits in a person, and again usually carries a positive sense.

Shiyam, the plural of shima, is similar to shamāʾil. Ordinary people use it as a synonym for honour, gallantry, and generosity. Someone might appeal to another by saying, “O man of honour.”

Iraqis have a saying: “Appeal to the peasant’s honour and take his cloak.”

In other words, stir his sense of pride and generosity and he will give you even the cloak from his own shoulders, though he owns nothing else.

Here gharami means the peasant or Bedouin, as distinct from the town-dweller, the city man who—according to the joke—has no such sense of honour.

Sufi ethics has three main sources:

pre-Islamic Arab values — Islamic teachings — Christian ethics.

Among the basic values inherited from the pre-Islamic period and broadly accepted by the Sufis were the following.

Noncooperation

This means rejecting the state, resisting it, and refusing submission to it.

It is a social and political position, and we have already discussed it in the preceding Orbits.

Dignity

Abd al-Qadir al-Jili says in Futuh al-Ghayb:

Be the servant of the Lord, not the servant of other human beings.

This expresses one of the worldly purposes of worshipping God, as it developed in both Christianity and Islam: a human being should be a servant of God, not the servant of another human being.

Sovereignty belongs to God alone. God is the only master.

Human beings are equal in their servitude to God. One cannot properly become the slave of another.

The obvious difficulty is slavery itself, where one human being is legally the master of another.

Jesus dealt with this by abolishing slavery in practice within the community of his movement. Its members were absolutely equal: neither wealth nor mastery gave one superiority over another.

But he did not dare issue a formal declaration abolishing slavery because he had to avoid direct confrontation with the Roman Empire.

As for Muhammad, one report in Shiite sources says that he considered abolishing slavery altogether (Makarim al-Akhlaq by the younger al-Tabrisi), but he did not do so.

Muhammad was pragmatic. His politics rested on balances and compromises, and his reason was stronger than his heart.

Still, he tried to lessen the suffering of slaves. He gave them rights unavailable under other slave systems. He prohibited beating and harming them, overworking them, and starving them. Masters were required to feed slaves from the same food they themselves ate, without distinction.

He even introduced a different language for speaking about them. Instead of saying “slave,” one was to say “young man” or “young woman.” A master speaking of a male or female slave should say “my young man” or “my young woman,” rather than “my slave” or “my bondwoman.”

It was a compromise between the slave’s right to freedom and the master’s supposed “right” of ownership.

The Sufis, for their part, did not call for the abolition of slavery either.

Instead they held to the principle of moral character, applying it to everyone: slave and free, Muslim and non-Muslim alike. In moral terms they gave them equal rights.

They also abolished slavery in their own personal lives. The great Sufi masters, in the overwhelming majority of cases, did not own male or female slaves.

This practice goes back to Abu Dharr al-Ghifari and Ruzbeh al-Isfahani—Salman the Persian—both of whom forbade themselves from owning slaves.

Each, however, had a freed woman who served him.

I have not been able to discover where these women came from: whether they had been purchased, or given to them as gifts and then freed, after which they remained as free servants.

I wish they had done without this service altogether. Even when it exists outside the legal institution of slavery, domestic service still carries something of slavery’s smell.

I mentioned in the previous Orbit that I included in the programme of my communalist organisation a demand for a law forbidding citizens from working as domestic servants in private homes.

Modern communist systems never achieved this.

It must be achieved under the communalist systems that will be built on grassroots communism, rather than communism imposed from above.

And, God willing, we will begin from this book.

Human dignity—personal honour—is almost as central a Sufi concern as divine love.

In Awarif al-Ma’arif, dignity is defined as:

A person’s knowledge of his own true worth, and his refusal to lower it for immediate worldly gain.

Their concern with dignity was so exacting that they distinguished between receiving obligatory alms and accepting voluntary charity.

A poor person, they said, may take what is due from the obligatory alms, but should not take voluntary charity.

Why?

Because obligatory alms are a legal right. No one can claim personal credit for giving them. They are taken from the rich by obligation, if necessary by force. The poor person who receives them has therefore received something by virtue of his own right, not through the generosity of the rich.

Voluntary charity is different. It comes as a gift from the wealthy person, and with it can come condescension, favouritism, or even bribery. Accepting it can injure a person’s dignity or compromise his independence.

I once found myself facing a similar problem in China over a passport.

Some friends offered to obtain one for me through the Iraqi embassy there. I refused.

I told them:

“I will accept it in one of two ways. Either I raid the embassy and take it by force, or I bribe one of its employees to get it for me. In the first case I will have obtained it through my own strength, and in the second through my own money.”

Our masters suffered greatly under the burden of this idea of dignity.

Bishr al-Hafi said:

What is lawful cannot bear extravagance, and taking from people is humiliation.

According to Ibn Asakir’s biography of him, Bishr made handkerchiefs with his own hands, sold them, and lived on the proceeds.

Their preference for manual work rested on two principles: refusal of the state and preservation of dignity.

Some took this to an extreme and rejected not only financial help but even personal favours.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi, as quoted by al-Sulami in the Tabaqat, said:

There is no burden in this world heavier than a favour. Whoever does you a kindness has tied you down; whoever neglects you has set you free.

(al-Sulami, p. 219)

He meant the sense of obligation created when someone does something for you. You then feel indebted to him.

This is why they said that the Sufi is someone who has no need of other people.

Yet he is also someone who serves other people and meets their needs.

One Sufi would refuse invitations to banquets from his friends, saying:

Waiting for the gravy is humiliation.

He meant the humiliation of sitting in another man’s house waiting for the food to arrive.

Food is not worth waiting for. A Sufi eats because he needs to, not for pleasure. A need should be met simply, with whatever happens to be available, without ceremony or elaborate preparation.

If he sits waiting for food, he becomes like a hungry man staring into the faces of those who will feed him and waiting for them to do so.

Ibn Sirin took a middle course. If he was invited to a meal, he would drink some sawiq at home first so that he would not arrive hungry.

Dignity, however, is not absolute.

A Sufi should show dignity before rulers, rich people, and the powerful.

Toward the poor, the opposite applies: he should humble himself.

Abu Uthman al-Hiri of Nishapur said:

To hold yourself high before the rich is humility, and to humble yourself before the poor is honour.

(al-Sulami, p. 175)

In modern terms, this means preserving the independence of culture in the face of state power and money, while surrendering that superiority before ordinary people.

The reverse is unacceptable: surrendering intellectual independence to the state while acting superior to ordinary people because “we are educated and they are illiterate.”

Dignity was a pre-Islamic Arab principle that Islam accepted, but Islam restricted it to believers:

Honour belongs to God, His Messenger, and the believers.

The Sufis made it universal. They extended dignity to all creation.

One consequence of dignity is that a person should ask nothing from anyone.

This must be watched carefully, not only in the obvious form of direct begging, but also in indirect forms—even vague sentences that might be interpreted as a request or as announcing some need.

Al-Qushayri reports this instruction from Abu Turab al-Nakhshabi to his disciples:

Whoever among you has no patched cloak has already asked. Whoever sits in a khanqah21 or a mosque has already asked. Whoever reads the Quran from a written copy where people can see or hear him has already asked.

The issue here is not dignity alone.

There is also the principle that a person must not join the Sufi path in pursuit of gain, prestige, or status.

The demands reinforce one another. A person cannot be genuinely self-respecting and opportunistic at the same time.

Relations with People and the Sufi Personality

Moral character is the goal of the Sufi’s striving.

His annihilation in God is also an annihilation in creation.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri describes the Sufi’s relations with others like this. He is:

a helper to the stranger, a father to the orphan, a husband to the widow, gentle with the poor, and someone people can turn to in every hardship.

In everyday dealings with people, he is cheerful and welcoming.

To call him “a husband to the widow” means that he helps make up for the support she has lost with her husband, so that she is not left dependent and unprotected.

And by cheerfulness and warmth we mean an easy personality, free of the psychological knots of religious men, the arrogance of state officials and the rich, and the educated person’s habit of looking down on ordinary people.

Abd al-Qadir al-Jili listed the elements of the Sufi personality by assigning to it qualities scattered among the prophets:

generosity from Abraham, patience from Job, gesture from Zechariah, estrangement from John, wool from Moses, wandering from Jesus, and poverty from Muhammad (Futuh al-Ghayb, p. 124).

This is, of course, an Islamic projection onto those figures, giving them qualities drawn from stories in the Torah or from reports passed down by Jewish rabbis.

The “gesture” of Zechariah refers to his three-day silence, during which he communicated by signs.

As for the estrangement of John the Baptist, I do not know what is meant beyond the fact that he was unjustly killed.

Moses did not wear wool. He lived more like a king.

Muhammad was not poor except in Mecca. Perhaps what was meant was simplicity of life, and that Muhammad certainly had.

Christ’s wandering was part of preaching his message, and it did not extend beyond the towns of Palestine.

Still, the Sufi personality that combines generosity, patience, asceticism, and poverty is, in this sense, a prophetic personality.

There is some ambiguity in the idea of generosity, because generosity assumes that one possesses money to give away.

The Sufi is not supposed to possess money.

Still, he can practise generosity with whatever happens to come into his hands.

One example is the futuh: unsolicited gifts from wealthy people sympathetic to Sufism. A shaykh might accept such gifts and then distribute them among the poor.

One story about Ibn Arabi says that a Turkish ruler in Anatolia gave him a magnificent palace worth one hundred thousand dirhams.

Ibn Arabi lived in it for a time.

Then a beggar came asking him for something.

At that moment Ibn Arabi had nothing else to give, so he gave the man the entire palace and walked out.

I believe the story.

The madness of the Sufis in conduct is the same madness we find in their speech.

We have already seen, however, that Ibn Arabi did accept gifts from rulers, unlike the great masters of social Sufism. He distributed most of what he received and kept only enough to support his family. He had two sons and a daughter.

The quality of “gesture” may also mean economy in speech and a preference for silence. The Sufis were not fond of long speeches or chatter.

The Sufi’s estrangement comes from seeing what others do not see. He is therefore a stranger in his own homeland.

Wandering points to their constant movement and travel.

Travel is one of the enduring urges of civilised people.

Islam also gives it a special emphasis through the principle of migration:

Whoever migrates in the path of God will find many places of refuge on the earth, and abundance.

The original meaning of migration here is defiance: challenging the source of persecution in one’s homeland. The first migration was from Mecca to Medina.

Wandering is migration at any time and from any place that has become too narrow for a person, allowing him to find freedom elsewhere.

When I left Baghdad twenty years ago, my migration was an act of defiance toward those who had seized control of it, not a search for comfort.

We have prophetic sayings encouraging travel, and others discouraging it or showing little enthusiasm for it.

The first were probably invented by merchants and Sufis, the second by jurists.

Chinese Muslims circulate a saying about travel in two forms:

Whoever dies a stranger dies a martyr.

And:

The death of a stranger is martyrdom.

The saying used to be written on the tombs of early Muslims in China before their descendants became fully settled there. The latest examples I have seen date from the middle of the eighth Islamic century.

Those who came to China during the Islamic period included merchants, ordinary travellers, and political refugees.

In one Chinese museum I saw a pottery figure of an Arab traveller, which suggests that such travellers were common in China at the time.

Travel became one of the marks of Sufi life. For this reason they established lodges where travelling Sufis—and other travellers as well—could stay free of charge.

It is said that Ibrahim al-Khawwas never remained in a single town for more than forty days.

The number forty is not meant literally here. Such numbers are often used simply to suggest either a short or a long period, and in this case it means a short one.

On his journeys he carried a water flask, a robe, and a needle.

He carried no food. He ate whatever he found along the way.

Even that was more luggage than Jesus is said to have carried. Christ had only a comb and a cup.

Then he threw away the cup when he saw someone drinking from a river with his hands.

And he threw away the comb when he saw someone combing his beard with his fingers.

Al-Ghazali devoted an entire book of more than a hundred large pages in the Ihya to travel.

Travel, of course, is not exclusive to the Sufis. As I said, it is one of the urges of civilised people. A great deal of poetry has been written about it outside Sufi literature.

Another moral quality expected of the Sufi is gentleness toward people, together with a refusal to oppress or attack them.

By “people” I mean ordinary people: creation, the Sufis’ people, the general public—not rulers and the rich.

In his commentary on Nahj al-Balagha, Ibn Abi al-Hadid quotes a Christian-like teaching attributed to Junayd:

The knower is not truly a knower until he is like the earth, walked upon by both the righteous and the wicked; like the cloud, giving shade to everything; and like the rain, watering what grows and what does not grow.

In other words, he deals generously with both decent and indecent people.

This does not mean kindness toward corrupt rulers and wealthy men. It means tolerance toward people whose conduct differs from your own in matters of religion and personal behaviour.

The great jurists22 distinguished between violating the rights of God and violating the rights of other human beings.

They held that the first category should be treated with tolerance, while the second required strictness.

Violations of God’s rights include neglect of acts of worship and personal prohibitions such as drinking wine or committing adultery.

Violations of people’s rights include oppression, theft, murder, assault, and anything else that harms another person’s interests or rights.

These must be treated much more seriously.

Within this distinction, Sufyan al-Thawri—as we mentioned earlier—would not even look at the palaces of the rich or of state officials. This was an extension of the principle of refusing contact with them.

At the same time, he dealt normally with sinners such as drinkers and libertines.

He even praised the conduct of the young ayyars, bands who specialised in robbing the rich and government officials.

Sufyan is counted by the Sufis among the prophets of Sufism, even though he lived before Sufism appeared as a movement.

Junayd’s phrase “like the cloud giving shade to everything” means serving all people without asking about their religion or beliefs.

And his phrase “like the rain, watering what grows and what does not grow” means doing good for those who deserve it and those who do not.

It resembles the popular saying today:

Do good and throw it into the river.

In other words, do not wait to be rewarded for kindness.

This teaching is Islamic but derives from Christianity.

The pre-Islamic Arabs did not approve of helping someone who did not deserve help. Zuhayr says in his famous ode:

Whoever does good for one unworthy of it will see his praise turn to blame, and will regret it.

The prophetic tradition revised this:

Do good to those who deserve it and those who do not. If the person you help does not deserve good, you yourself are still one of those who do.

All this concerns service to people in ordinary life.

Junayd’s teaching also calls for decent treatment of people despite differences in conduct and belief—with the exception, again, of rulers, the wealthy, and those who spread corruption.

The Sufi is expected to repair whatever fault he sees in another person, covering for him and concealing his shortcomings.

Hamdan al-Qassar expressed this beautifully:

If you see a drunk man, stagger yourself, so that you do not become arrogant toward him and then find yourself tested by the same thing.

The point is that you should display in yourself the defect you see in another person, so that you do not imagine yourself superior to him, and so that you can help protect him from ridicule and humiliation.

The Sufis were extremely sensitive about such things. They were anxious not to hurt people because of mistakes or embarrassing accidents.

One story tells of a woman who came to Hatim al-Asamm to ask him a question.

While she was there, she accidentally passed wind.

She froze in embarrassment.

Hatim immediately said:

“Speak louder.”

He pretended to be deaf.

The woman relaxed because she believed he had not heard what had happened.

Hatim was an Afghan from Balkh. When he came to Baghdad, his Arabic carried a heavy accent. Yet no one could debate him without being defeated by his argument.

Some Baghdadis asked him how this was possible when he was a foreigner and spoke Arabic with difficulty.

He replied:

“I have three qualities. I am happy when my opponent is right. I am sad when he is wrong. And I guard myself against treating him ignorantly”—meaning that he would not insult or abuse him in argument.

What people today call democratic dialogue, Hatim regarded as the reason he could defeat an opponent.

Stories like this about the Sufi masters were circulated in Sufi books for educational purposes. They understood that an example or a story can teach more effectively than a long sermon.

Sufi conduct also requires relationships free of needless ceremony and formality.

A Sufi should be easy company. He should not burden the people around him or force them to manage his moods. He should not be an unpleasant guest.

As Dhu al-Nun al-Misri put it, he should be cheerful and welcoming.

They disliked excessive politeness.

Qut al-Qulub says that the earlier generations, when they met one another, rarely said more than:

“How are you?”

or:

“How are all of you?”

They also disapproved of prying into other people’s affairs.

It was considered contrary to proper conduct to meet someone in the road and ask:

“Where are you going?”

or:

“Where have you come from?”

If a Sufi knocked at someone’s door, he would pause for a little while to make sure the person inside was ready to receive him.

They had no way of arranging appointments beforehand.

If permission to enter was not given, he simply left without becoming upset.

Riyah al-Qaysi once suffered a severe crisis of conscience after visiting a friend and finding him asleep.

He criticised the man for sleeping.

Then he realised what he had said.

He went off to the cemetery and began rebuking himself.

This belongs to what they called self-accounting—what people today would call self-criticism—carried out privately between a person and himself.

Alongside this, or completing it, was indifference to what other people said about you.

Praise and blame should become equal.

The Sufi himself neither praises nor condemns—again, meaning ordinary people, not rulers and the rich. He certainly condemns rulers, wealthy men, and soldiers, and naturally does not praise them.

He may, however, praise an ordinary person who deserves it, in order to encourage good qualities.

Indifference to praise and blame is one measure of strength in the Sufi personality.

It also expresses independence: the seeker refuses to submit to social standards he considers false or inauthentic.

A man once asked Abu Yazid al-Bistami how he might attain inner peace.

Abu Yazid told him to go out into the market riding a stick like a hobbyhorse, running along while children shouted after him.

The point was to destroy his solemn public image, break pride within him, and free him from the obsession with reputation and status.

They also cited Umar ibn al-Khattab, who used to walk quickly and say that walking quickly got things done and kept him further from vanity.

This conflicts with a saying that claims:

Walking quickly takes away the believer’s dignity.

But reports of Umar’s quick pace are strengthened by Aisha’s description of him: whenever he walked, she said, he moved fast.

Umar was tall and his feet turned outward. When he walked, he looked almost as though he were riding while everyone else was walking.

Members of ruling families, beginning with the Umayyads, had a special gait they trained themselves to use.

Tyrannical rulers, rich men, and military officers likewise have a way of walking marked by heaviness and swagger.

The Sufis wanted the walk of ordinary people: natural, without ceremony or display.

Another requirement of Sufi independence is that the Sufi must not worship his teachers.

That does not mean failing to respect and honour them. A teacher has rights over a student.

It means refusing to believe that the teacher is infallible.

A disciple needs a teacher.

Al-Bistami said:

Whoever has no shaykh has Satan for a shaykh.

But the disciple should receive his teacher’s teaching with an awake mind. Education should not be rote indoctrination. It should be understood and absorbed.

At the same time, they discouraged constant argument with the teacher because it showed poor manners and could make teaching impossible.

But education has a limit.

In Futuh al-Ghayb that point is called the stage of weaning. The disciple separates from his teacher and becomes a teacher in his own right.

Tolerance is a central ethical principle in the Sufi personality.

We have already seen how it works in everyday social relations.

But it also applies to questions of belief.

We have discussed the principle of equal rights among religions, and between religious and non-religious people.

Abd al-Qadir al-Jili is particularly strict on the question of declaring people unbelievers.

Among the qualities required of people undergoing spiritual discipline, he says, is this:

Never state with certainty that any person who belongs to the Muslim community is guilty of idolatry, unbelief, or hypocrisy. This is closer to mercy, higher in rank, more faithful to the Prophetic way, and further from intruding into God’s knowledge.

(Futuh al-Ghayb, p. 128, discourse 78.)

Al-Jili raised the matter because he was a jurist as well as a Sufi.

His statement is therefore also a legal judgment against declaring people unbelievers.

Most jurists did not agree, though some leading ones did. Taj al-Din al-Subki, for example, agreed that a Muslim should not be declared an unbeliever merely because of an opinion he expresses.

He limited such rulings to explicit apostasy: openly leaving Islam and entering another religion.

When dealing with people of different religions and different forms of religious conduct, al-Jili also told his disciples never to consider themselves better than anyone else.

A Sufi should deal with sinful or immoral Muslims, and with non-Muslims, on the assumption that they may all be better than he is.

Why?

Because the sinner may repent while he himself later falls into sin.

And the non-Muslim may become Muslim while he himself leaves Islam.

(Futuh al-Ghayb, p. 129.)

Through teachings like these, the Sufis confronted a deep problem in the religious personality: the tendency to see itself as superior to everyone else and to claim exclusive possession of truth and virtue.

The Sufi is open toward people who differ from him in conduct or belief.

He does not pursue people by branding them sinful, heretical, or unbelieving.

In the same spirit, the Sufis rejected the excessive ritualism of Islam and tried to reduce its weight.

As we saw in earlier Orbits, they criticised acts of worship and even accused the prophets of burdening people with too many obligations.

Al-Sha’rani says in Tanbih al-Mughtarrin that among their ethical principles was this:

spending money to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and pay the debts of people unable to repay them should take priority over building Sufi lodges, religious houses, and similar structures—that is, over building mosques. (p. 168)

Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said:

A mouthful of food in the stomach of a hungry person weighs more heavily in my scale than the building of a mosque.

Sufi books say a great deal about trust in God, and they give it different meanings.

Some interpreted it passively: a person should not pursue livelihood too aggressively, because livelihood comes from God.

This view is usually found among Sufis closer to Sunni orthodoxy.

But the more common Sufi position is expressed in the Prophet’s saying:

Tie your camel, then trust in God.

He is said to have told this to a Bedouin who asked whether he could leave his camel untied and rely on God to protect it.

The general principle is simple:

work first, trust second.

In this order, trust in God is psychological. It helps a person deal with the effects of failure, so that disappointment does not destroy him or darken his spirit.

It also encourages him to keep working, because he feels that God remains with him.

The Sufis made work a duty.

They required the disciple to earn a living before devoting himself fully to Sufism. He was not permitted simply to wait for someone else to feed him.

As we have already seen, the best livelihood in their eyes was that earned by one’s own hands—the work of craftsmen and wage labourers.

In the section on proper social conduct in the Ihya, al-Ghazali says:

The purest food a servant of God can eat is what a craftsman earns with his own hands, provided he works honestly.

That is, provided he does not cheat in his craft.

Among their instructions to disciples, as reported by al-Qushayri, was this:

Whoever desires what ordinary people desire must obtain it in the way ordinary people obtain it: through the labour of his hands and the sweat of his brow.

(p. 183.)

They also gave “trust in God” characteristically Sufi interpretations, often stretching words beyond their obvious meaning.

Qut al-Qulub defines it as:

The heart’s stillness toward what people possess, and the ending of concern with what lies in their hands.

In other words: not needing other people and not longing for what they own.

Another definition says:

No one reaches the station of trust until praise and blame from other people become equal to him.

(2/5–9.)

This adds another element to the personality we have already been describing.

Do not care excessively about what other people say about you, so long as you know yourself, recognise your own faults, and judge yourself honestly.

There is also a streak of madness in the Sufi personality, just as there is in Sufi speech.

We have already discussed it.

Seen in that light, the stories of Sufis giving away everything they owned and living instead from manual work—or from the very little required for survival—become perfectly believable.

We need not be surprised that Ibrahim ibn Adham handed over ten thousand dinars to the slave whom his family sent to him after his father’s death, then freed the man and continued earning his own living by harvesting crops and cleaning.

Nor need we be surprised that Yusuf ibn Asbat inherited seventy thousand dirhams and refused to take any of it.

Or that Ibn Arabi gave his royal palace to a beggar, as though determined to outdo his ancestor Hatim, who slaughtered his only horse when he had nothing else with which to feed a guest.

Ibn Arabi was proud of this connection and called himself al-Hatimi.

When the Sufi speaks of absolute unity, he also applies that unity to the intimate bond between thought and conduct.

The two become one in their madness, in their departure from the logic accepted by the surrounding world.

And once he reaches that point, he does not care if people throw stones at him.

Ordering Rights and Duties

Al-Harith al-Muhasibi, a third-century figure and one of the masters of Sunni Sufism, arranged a number of basic rights and duties in the following order:

  • A mother’s claim to care comes before a father’s. A child should attend to his mother first because she is usually more in need of care.

  • Supporting one’s family comes before pilgrimage or the lesser pilgrimage. A person must first secure his family’s livelihood before travelling to Mecca.

  • A debt that has fallen due comes before pilgrimage. If someone owes money and payment is due, he should not go on pilgrimage. He must pay the debt first, and then perform the pilgrimage if he can still afford to do so.

  • A wife’s rights come before satisfying one’s parents.

Al-Muhasibi does not say that a wife’s rights come before the rights of one’s parents. He says they come before pleasing them.

This is precise.

A wife’s rights and the rights of parents are equally binding. One set of rights cannot simply be cancelled for the sake of the other.

But parental approval is something different.

Parents may treat a wife unjustly. In that case, her rights cannot be violated merely to keep them happy.

This follows the Quranic teaching:

If they pressure you to associate with Me what you have no knowledge of, do not obey them; but continue to live with them in this world with kindness.

Parents may order someone to do wrong. They may themselves act unjustly. They are not to be obeyed in such matters, while their legitimate rights are still preserved.

Al-Harith gives another instruction on the same subject.

A person must not please his parents by cutting off relatives.

Parents may be involved in grudges and disputes with other members of the family. Their child is not therefore permitted to withhold help or service from those relatives simply to satisfy them.

  • Friday prayer comes before returning a deposit held in trust.

This belongs to the rights of worship.

Perhaps al-Muhasibi assumed that delaying the return of the deposit until after prayer would cause no harm.

Otherwise the ruling would conflict with the general principle that one should be lenient in matters involving God’s rights and strict in matters involving the rights of people.

Al-Muhasibi has other teachings as well. Among the most important are these:

  • Do not beat or humiliate your children to please your wife.

The child meant here is a child from another wife who has died or been divorced.

Some fathers mistreat such children in order to please a new wife.

Women in this situation can sometimes lose all compassion and acquire a harshness almost military in character, making it difficult to apply to them the old description “the gentle sex.”

Al-Harith al-Muhasibi recognised these realities and tried to deal with them through his Sufi moral sense.

  • Do not fulfil moral obligations using suspect money.

By obligatory rights he means money a person is required to provide to parents, relatives, or some public interest.

“Suspect money” means wealth tainted by illegality: money obtained through seizure, embezzlement, bribery, or similar means.

Much of what Sufis accepted from rulers fell into this category.

The poet alludes to the contradiction:

Like a woman seeking to do good with money earned from selling her body— damn you, neither fornicate nor give alms.

The Sufis had no settled position on distributing money stolen from the rich in the manner of the ayyars.

And Abd al-Qadir al-Jili’s call to seize wealth and distribute it among the poor remains too vague to tell us exactly what he had in mind.

Guidance for Solving a Problem

In the fourth discourse of Futuh al-Ghayb, al-Jili gives three successive options for dealing with a problem.

The first is to rely on yourself.

Try to solve the problem through your own abilities and resources.

If you cannot solve it yourself, turn to other people: the state and its employees, people with influence or wealth, respected figures in society—or doctors, if you are ill.

If none of them can solve the problem, then turn to your Lord through prayer and supplication.

The sequence is deliberate:

so long as you can help yourself, do not turn to other people;

so long as other people can help you, do not turn to the Creator.

Several basic principles of life follow from this teaching.

1. Rely on yourself first, and try not to depend on others.

2. It is permissible to seek the state’s help in solving a personal problem.

This does not contradict the principle of keeping one’s distance from the state.

The governed have rights over the state, and they are entitled to demand them.

Security is an obvious example. If someone is attacked, he may turn to the authorities to stop the attacker.

In disputes of every kind, the state may have to intervene through the police and courts.

But what about asking the state for financial help?

An ordinary person has the right to do so.

A Sufi, a jurist, or any other learned person—that is, anyone we would now call an intellectual—does not.

It is useful to keep one distinction in mind.

The principle of noncooperation with the state is binding on the intellectual, not on ordinary people.

The exception is when an organised movement is under way to remove a ruler and ordinary people have joined it. At that point, the ordinary participant has effectively become a political or union activist and must also refrain from contact or cooperation with the state.

Something like this happened during the reform movement, when the people of Baghdad mobilised against al-Muqtadir and his minister Hamid ibn al-Abbas.

At that point, any person who established contact with the caliph or his minister was effectively breaking with the collective position.

Similar questions arose in the modern Iraqi national movement, first led by jurists and later by communists. They were really continuations of old traditions of political opposition.

When Shaykh Mahdi al-Khalisi issued a ruling calling for a boycott of King Faisal’s government, any politician who accepted a ministerial or administrative office came to be accused of betrayal.

But no one objected when an ordinary citizen submitted a petition asking the state to stop an assault, remove an injustice, or remedy some harm.

The same general pattern has continued to the present day.

3. Turning to God and placing one’s trust in Him comes only after one has lost hope of solving the problem by ordinary means.

The sequence ends in surrender to God.

From this we can understand God’s action as bringing peace to the heart of the desperate person, so that despair does not destroy him.

Summary

The Sufi personality is positive, not negative.

It acts as much as it receives.

It remains open to life even while renouncing sensual pleasures and turning away from luxury.

The Sufi is free.

He loves nature, and for that reason he travels. Wandering is one of the foundations of his freedom.

That freedom rests on other foundations as well, the first of which is renunciation:

own nothing, so that nothing can own you.

The Sufi is independent.

He follows no one blindly, obeys no one absolutely, and imitates no one.

He has self-respect. He guards his dignity and his human essence.

He is hard toward those who dominate others: rulers, wealthy men, and soldiers.

Toward ordinary people he is tolerant. He loves them, defends them, and serves them.

He is not fanatical about a religious school, a religion, or a group.

He does not pursue people by calling them foolish or inferior.

He does not condemn ordinary people. His condemnation is directed toward rulers, the rich, and soldiers.

He may praise an ordinary person to encourage upright conduct, but he does not praise those in power.

He is free of malice without being naive.

Peaceful without being weak.

He smiles at people, but his heart is sad and full of cares.

The Sufi also cares about cleanliness, sometimes to an extreme.

It is said that Abu Yazid al-Bistami had three sets of clothes: one for going outside, one for wearing at home, and a third for entering the lavatory.

The same was true of his shoes.

Flies were said not to approach Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani because he was so clean and used perfume.

Yet he sat with the poor and picked lice from their clothes.

He did this because he could not provide them with proper means of cleanliness, so he shared the burden with them himself.

Some Sufis, however, discouraged excessive bathing. Such figures seem to have been influenced by Indian asceticism.

The Sufi speaks little.

He does not indulge in endless disputes or insist on argument.

They often repeat a saying attributed to Ma’ruf al-Karkhi and others:

When God wishes good for a people, He opens the door of action and closes the door of argument. When He wishes the opposite, He opens the door of argument and closes the door of action.

The Sufi is sensitive.

He does not burden anyone.

People do not feel uncomfortable in his company.

He makes no grand claims and does not boast.

He sees himself as less than others and does not believe that anyone owes him recognition for his virtues.

He is honest with himself and with other people.

For that reason, he does not remain fixed in one state. He changes constantly as new truths become visible to him.

Junayd expressed this by saying:

The truthful person changes forty times in a day. The hypocrite remains in one condition for forty years.

Why?

Because the Sufi accepts truth when it comes from another person, while recognising error when it comes from himself and correcting it.

He learns from what he reads and from what he experiences, developing both his ideas and his practice.

This quality belongs to the great intellectual—the universal intellectual.

It marks a movement from merely being shaped by things to becoming someone capable of shaping them: from being governed by the world to becoming capable of judging it.

The Palestinian critic Yusuf Sami al-Yusuf once published an essay on Sufism in which he discussed Sufi ethics and argued for its superiority to the ethics of the German philosopher Immanuel Kant.

His reason was that Sufi ethics contains a living, active element, whereas Kant’s ethics, in his view, remains purely abstract, rigid, and alienated from life.

This is really a broader problem with philosophers and ethics, including the philosophers of Islam.

Their ethics tends to consist more of abstract moral instruction than of living ethical systems.

Abu Bakr al-Razi’s Philosophical Life took a more practical direction because it began from his own conduct and his life as a doctor and philosopher.

Al-Razi shared something of the Sufi spirit in his deistic spirituality, which rejected organised religion, and in his relationship with ordinary people: he served them through medicine and defended them in his philosophy.

He founded the independent line in Islamic philosophy.

Greek teachers did not exercise a one-way influence over him. His metaphysical system also drew on Eastern sources, which he developed through his own creative approach.

Al-Razi could easily be placed among the Abdal: those exemplary figures who respected ordinary people, defended them, and served them through their own field of expertise.

But the philosophical way of life described by al-Razi is not typical of philosophers in general, especially in European philosophy beginning with the Greeks.

Few Greek or modern European philosophers combined the roles of philosopher and sage.

Most lived ordinary lives with little in their conduct to distinguish them from anyone else.

Their relationship with ordinary people was blocked by the complexity of their thought and by their intellectual aristocracy.

The same is true of the philosophers of Islam.

They had little relationship with ordinary people, though their personal lives varied.

Al-Farabi and al-Shirazi were spiritually inclined.

Ibn Sina was pleasure-loving.

Most of the others lived ordinary lives, without anything especially distinctive in their stance or conduct.

A Warning and a Reminder

Adonis drew a sharp comparison between Sufism and Surrealism from several angles.

Both break out into the space of the irrational and the limitless.

Both rebel against reality, its social conventions, and the laws imposed by the state.

Both seek the human freedom that existed before the state enslaved the human being.

But from what Adonis himself writes about Surrealism in his important book Sufism and Surrealism, I have come to believe that Surrealism bears a considerable share of responsibility for the disintegration visible in the West today.

It provided an ideology for an unrestrained idea of freedom: the idea that the individual may realise his individuality at any moment, in any place, by any means; that every barrier standing before overwhelming desire should be smashed in the name of freedom; that the body should become the vehicle of experiment.

Under this logic, unrestricted sex merges with divine love, and killing according to personal whim is joined to rejection of the state.

From there one enters the theatre of organised crime.

Sufi ethics has nothing to do with this.

Different doctrines must not be carelessly mixed together.

Adonis should have approached the Western text cautiously—with his own critical caution, not in the manner of translators.

Sufism seeks to build a good world free of religion, superstition, the state, and aggression.

A free world.

But one governed by values people accept voluntarily.

In such a world, a person does not kill because he feels like it.

Nor is a woman’s body violated in the name of rebellion against the family.

When the Sufi loves a woman, she becomes spiritual in his eyes.

In that spiritualisation, human love and divine love merge into one another.

Postscript

The letters have informed me that one reason for the extreme emphasis some Sufis placed on trust in God was the fierce greed of the rich and of state officials in accumulating wealth.

Some Sufis responded by stressing renunciation in order to counter that drive.

This negative or passive tendency does not appear in other matters such as seeking knowledge, struggle, or resistance to the three powers.

Farewell to the Orbit of Zayn al-Abidin

During the Battle of Siffin between Ali and Muawiya, Muawiya seized the only usable watering place on that stretch of the Euphrates and prevented Ali’s army from reaching it.

Ali organised an attack, drove Muawiya’s forces away, and took control of the water.

But then he ordered that a path be opened so that Muawiya’s men could come down to the river and drink.

This was an extreme application of moral rules in war.

Ali would have been within his rights to deny the enemy water and use thirst as a means of forcing them to surrender.

The ethical rules of war should go no further than prohibiting treacherous weapons of surprise—which in ancient times meant burning and poisoning, both forbidden in Islam—and requiring humane treatment of prisoners.

No more than that.

The Orbit of Orbits

Some Sufi Terms

The Sufis broke with ordinary, logical ways of writing. They plunged into madness, linguistic delirium, and strained interpretation. They also broke free of the limits imposed by dictionaries and grammar. They drew new meanings out of existing words, sometimes through an obvious connection, sometimes through a distant one, and sometimes with no visible connection at all. They coined new words from roots and derivatives, bending language to their purposes.

They paid little attention to the grammarians. To them, grammarians belonged to the outside world. The grammarian and the Sufi had no common ear with which to hear one another and no common tongue with which to speak.

They made context, not dictionary meaning or grammatical form, decide what a word meant. Some of their terms never settled on a single meaning at all. They used them according to what the argument required at that moment, which is why their own explanations of these terms often differ.

Here are some of them, drawn from al-Sarraj al-Tusi’s al-Lumaʿ and other works.

State: Something that descends on a person in a particular moment, remains briefly, then passes. Most Sufis held that a state does not last. A moment of clarity may flash into being and disappear almost at once. Joy, sadness, contraction, expansion, longing, anxiety, and stillness are all states.

Station: Something that becomes firmly established in a person and endures. Reaching a station requires effort and discipline. It may begin as a passing state, recur again and again, and eventually become permanent.

A station in this sense is what the existentialist philosopher Kierkegaard called an “eternal disposition.”

One station can also rise into a higher one. Stations include self-examination, love, asceticism, opposition, closeness to people, and bringing them comfort.

Place: The level reached by people who have attained perfection, firmness, and the final stages of the path. Once a person has completed the inner meanings and passed through states and stations, a lasting place becomes established for him.

The “place” is therefore the highest position, associated with the rank of the Pole.

Witnessing: Nearness and direct presence. It is close in meaning to unveiling, though unveiling is fuller.

At the beginning of witnessing, the marks of particular existence shine out through disclosures of presence, while still remaining beneath the cover of the unseen. The heart then seeks an unbroken presence with what the unseen has given it.

Witnessing means disclosure: seeing the truth, living it, and experiencing it directly rather than thinking about it. Thought belongs to reason and logic. Witnessing is seeing, touching, and living.

It belongs to the world of intuition, reached through contemplation and complete absorption in the hidden depths of existence.

Al-Qushayri says that by “unveiling” the Sufis may have meant something close to what a person sees in the state between waking and sleep.

This may also be one source of the delirium in which logic breaks apart and the distance between opposites disappears. The person in delirium stands somewhere between waking awareness and the hiddenness of intoxication.

Glimpses: Secrets that flash into view and lift the seeker upward from one state to a higher one. They appear during his progress, but they are fleeting and do not last.

After them come the gleams, which last longer, and then the rising lights, which are settled states.

Shares and rights: Rights are what a person is entitled to by religious law or accepted custom, especially what is needed for life and survival.

Shares are whatever lies beyond those rights. Among the Sufis they are usually spiritual things, such as mystical drinking or divine manifestation.

The two stand in tension. When rights appear, shares disappear; when shares appear, rights disappear.

The tension is between a person’s material rights and his spiritual shares. The higher a Sufi rises through the stages of nearness and manifestation, the more he gives up his own claims.

The elite of the elite: A rank reached by those who have crossed through the states and stations, travelled their paths, and passed through their deserts.

Allusion: Something whose meaning is too subtle for the speaker to reveal in a direct statement. It hints rather than explains.

Al-Rudhabari said:

Our knowledge is allusion. Once it becomes explicit statement, it disappears.

This is also what al-Niffari meant when he said:

The wider the vision, the narrower the words.

Language therefore has to be exceeded by allusion.

Here, “allusion” means symbol and whatever works like it. It does not mean bodily gesture. Bodily gesture is signalling.

Symbol: A hidden meaning stored beneath visible words, recognised only by those who belong to the tradition.

Al-Naqqad said:

When they speak, the reach of their symbols defeats you; when they fall silent, how far you are from reaching them.

The word in the first half-line violates the expected grammar. The Sufis did not care much about grammar.

Someone once said that if you want to understand the symbols of our masters, look through their letters and correspondence. Their real symbols are there, not in their formal books.

Unfortunately, almost none of their correspondence has survived.

Clarity: A state purified of interference from ordinary temperament, in which realities are seen as the acts of the Real in the present moment.

For some Sufis it simply means leaving blameworthy qualities behind.

The clarity of clarity: Passing beyond states and stations and entering the final stages.

It also means freeing the secrets from created things so that the Real is witnessed through the Real, continuously and without cause.

What is meant is the knower reaching the furthest limit of knowledge.

Gathering: A state of union in which the person sees nothing but the Real. Whoever still sees something other than the Real has not gathered.

It means that awareness of the Real completely takes possession of a person’s inner life. When he returns to ordinary action, he returns to separation.

We might put it this way:

Seeing acts is separation. Seeing attributes is gathering. Seeing the Essence is the gathering of gathering.

The gathering of gathering is annihilation.

There is also the eye of gathering, which is itself the eye of annihilation.

This level corresponds to pure unity: complete identification between the knower and the Real.

Some claimed that reaching it required leaving creed and religious law behind. Umar al-Suhrawardi rejected this. Gathering, he said, belongs to the spirit, while separation belongs to the human frame. As long as the human being remains made of both, gathering and separation must remain together.

In other words, the knower moves back and forth between moments of annihilation and moments of awareness. He does not dissolve completely.

What matters here is that the great Sufi masters did not accept release from the religious law, even though they had all moved beyond fixed creed.

Leaving religious law altogether would mean falling into lawlessness and permissiveness.

Al-Tahanawi tells us in his Kashshaf (1/116) that some false Sufis said:

We have no power to avoid sins or carry out commandments. No one in this world owns another person or another person’s labour. Everyone shares wealth and spouses alike.

They confused communal ownership of wealth with communal ownership of women.

The great masters of social Sufism accepted the first, not the second.

Those who preached this kind of permissiveness were minor Sufis who claimed to have reached absolute gathering and the furthest edge of knowledge. In reality they had not. Only the great ones reached it.

And the great ones did not abandon the rules of religion and ethics. They freed themselves from creeds and from fanaticism toward them.

They could ignore religious rules they rejected—slavery, polygamy, commerce—but they remained committed to other rules governing conduct, social relations, rights, and things that must not be violated.

According to al-Junayd, Abu Yazid reached the eye of gathering. He left creed behind, but he did not abandon the ethical obligations of religious law. In fact, he added moral obligations that the law itself did not contain.

He completed what it lacked.

Sobriety and intoxication: Two opposite states.

Intoxication is the astonishment that overtakes the lover when the beauty of the beloved suddenly appears before him. More generally, it means being overwhelmed by the power of a state.

It belongs to attraction and annihilation.

After intoxication comes sobriety: the knower returns to ordinary sensation after having been absent from it.

“Intoxication” is a metaphor for being so completely absorbed in contemplation that things being contemplated become disclosed.

Something like this can happen to any serious thinker absorbed in investigation. Among Sufis, however, it can become complete immersion in the cosmic spirit—in the divine Essence understood in the Sufi, rather than conventional religious, sense.

Then intoxication passes. A state, as we have said, does not last. The knower returns to sobriety.

It is in this return that knowledge reaches completion, because the intuitive disclosure produced by deep contemplation becomes fully realised.

This is the method of Sufi philosophy: intuition.

There are two kinds of sobriety.

The first comes before intoxication. It is the ordinary state shared by everyone.

The second comes after intoxication. In it the knower returns filled with majesty and beauty, together with the truths discovered during contemplation.

The second sobriety may not arrive immediately. The knower may pass through a process of fluctuation, moving back and forth between intoxication and sobriety until the state settles and becomes firm.

They also associated ecstatic utterance with intoxication.

An ecstatic utterance is a statement that breaks with creed. Many of the famous sayings attributed to Abu Yazid and al-Hallaj belong to this category. It is one of the features of irreligious Sufism.

But it can also appear in orthodox Sufism. There are many examples.

The truth is that ecstatic utterance is common to all the great Sufi masters, whatever category we place them in.

The ecstatic sayings of al-Jili the lover and al-Jili the grandson resemble one another. In the grandson they are spread out; in the ancestor they are brief.

Linking ecstatic utterance to intoxication can be a way of escaping responsibility for what was said. But the utterance also belongs to sobriety, because what the ecstatic says while intoxicated does not fundamentally change when he returns to sobriety.

That is what they mean when they say that the second sobriety is the summit of perfection.

Presence: Close in meaning to sobriety. Sobriety moves between intoxication and sobriety, while presence is continuous.

Presence belongs to the heart, not the body.

When Bishr al-Hafi was asked why he did not pray in the first row, he said:

I know what He wants. He wants hearts brought near, not bodies brought near.

They also said that presence can exist in absence.

Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri put it this way:

When I disappear, He appears; when He appears, He makes me disappear.

Rushing in and overpowering impulses: Someone seized by a powerful desire for what he seeks will rush toward it.

If he believes what he wants lies across a sea, he swims into the sea. If he believes it lies in a wilderness, he enters the wilderness.

When desire overwhelms him and the demand becomes strong enough, he may even throw himself into fire.

Whether this destroys him, costs him his life, brings him to what he seeks, or fails to bring him there makes no difference.

This is an answer to outsiders who treat Sufism as pure negation, and treat Tao in the same way.

No. As our master Abd al-Qadir said:

In every field of glory they rise to a lofty rank, and in every army they march at the head of the procession.

Annihilation and abiding: These have many definitions.

Annihilation can be relative or absolute. Absolute annihilation occurs when the power of reality completely takes possession of the knower, so that he disappears from his own interests and from everything else.

In al-Lumaʿ, annihilation is the disappearance of the self’s attributes, the disappearance of resistance, and coming to rest in the state that has descended.

Abiding means the endurance of annihilation.

The disappearance of the self’s qualities may be a passing state, or it may settle and remain for a long time.

There can also be annihilation in the Real, in which the qualities of the created being disappear into the qualities of the Creator.

This is the eye of gathering: the stage in which the human being becomes divine.

Many Sufis proclaimed it, among them al-Hallaj and Abu Yazid.

This stage corresponds to reaching the highest degree of strength.

Al-Hallaj was in such a state when he began his activity in Baghdad, was arrested, and was killed. He endured what was done to him almost as though he found sweetness in it.

Sufism is heroism—but not individual heroism.

It is courage—but not courage confined to the battlefield.

It is courage in the broadest sense: present at every moment, in every place, whoever may be standing before you.

It is not the courage of the soldier who fights the enemy and then returns obediently to his commander.

It is the courage of free people.

Annihilation has also been defined as complete absorption in the greatness of the Creator and the witnessing of the Real: that is, immersion in absolute existence and attachment to the spirit of the universe.

It is the highest degree of contemplation.

Beginner: Someone who begins the path with firm resolve. He is trained by someone who already knows the state.

Seeker: Someone whose beginning has proved genuine. He has entered the company of those who have cut themselves off from outside powers, and the hearts of the sincere testify to the truth of his intention.

But he has not yet acquired a state or station.

The sought one: The knower who no longer has a will of his own.

Before becoming the sought one, he is a traveller. The traveller comes after the seeker, or alongside him.

The knower is the person who has reached the final stages. He becomes sought after first having been a seeker.

Ecstasy: The heart suddenly recovering a purity of remembrance that had been lost.

Its substance is love overpowering the lover.

Longing and grief meet in it.

The Sufi’s longing contains sorrow. His love contains tears. His body suffers while his spirit rejoices.

If the person in ecstasy has a human beloved and is given the choice between meeting her and remaining apart, he chooses separation.

Meeting contains the possibility of complaint about the pain of longing. It also contains the possibility of physical union.

This is why the great Sufi does not marry the woman he loves. If he married her, ecstasy would turn into loss. The spirit would sink into ordinary affection and lose the power to carry him toward his cosmic throne.

Al-Wasiti said that ecstasy has four stages:

bewilderment, confusion, intoxication, and sobriety.

It is like someone who first hears about the sea, then approaches it, then enters it, then is seized by the waves, and finally emerges again.

Emerging corresponds to sobriety.

It belongs to those to whom the realities of the unseen have been disclosed.

Showing ecstasy: Making ecstasy visible.

It can also mean acting intoxicated, whether by imitation or by genuinely falling into intoxication.

This often happens during musical listening, when melody and words stir something in a person’s inner being, move him, and perhaps make him dance.

The knower, however, maintains his composure. Ecstasy does not show itself outwardly except when appropriate, and it does not draw attention to him.

We have already seen this in the story of al-Junayd at a gathering of music.

First stirring: What first appears in the heart at a particular moment, according to the knower’s state.

Incoming state: What comes into the heart after the first stirring and then absorbs it.

An incoming state has an action and an effect. The first stirring does not.

Some limited incoming states to praiseworthy things such as joy, sadness, contraction, and expansion.

The Sufis use the word joy, not exultation, because exultation can carry the sense of arrogance and excess.

Sudden visitations: Things that strike the heart unexpectedly and bring either expansion or contraction.

The word comes from the same root as badīha, sudden intuition, or at least shares its root.

In ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif, sudden knocks, first visitations, sudden visitations, rising lights, gleams, glimpses, and sparks are all treated as closely related terms.

We have already discussed glimpses.

They defined sudden knocks as things that strike the hearts of people of truth through hearing and renew their inner realities.

Some of these experiences may conflict with religious law.

Contraction and expansion: Two states of the knowers.

When the Real contracts them, they become reluctant to take advantage even of permitted pleasures such as food, drink, and similar things.

When the Real expands them, He returns them to these things.

That is one definition.

I smell opportunism in it.

Minor Sufis could use “expansion” as an excuse to enjoy permitted pleasures, and perhaps go beyond them as well.

Al-Junayd defined contraction and expansion as fear and hope.

Hope expands a person toward obedience.

Fear contracts him away from wrongdoing.

Contraction has also been defined by the saying:

Contraction for the knower is like fear for someone seeking safety.

In the “hidden station,” expansion means that God opens the knower outwardly toward people while drawing him inwardly toward Himself, as an act of mercy toward creation.

The idea is that the knower remains among people and looks after what is due to them, while giving up his own share for his Lord.

Bishr al-Hafi once applied this contrast to himself and Maʿruf al-Karkhi. The two lived at the same time and were close companions. Maʿruf attended banquets; Bishr did not.

Bishr said:

Maʿruf eats from the expansion of knowledge. I refrain from the contraction of scrupulousness.

Inner prompting: A message that enters the mind.

Sometimes it is cast into it by angels, sometimes by devils, sometimes by the self, and sometimes by God.

An inner prompting can therefore contain good or evil.

Angels symbolise what is good, as does God. Devils symbolise evil.

The devil is a symbol. He is not Iblis.

Iblis, after all, is one of their masters.

Indeed, he is the first Pole.

Knowledge of certainty: Knowledge based on evidence and proof.

It means theoretical knowledge founded on observation and reasoning.

Eye of certainty: Knowledge reached through disclosures and descending intuitions.

Truth of certainty: Knowledge reached by witnessing and direct seeing.

It is the highest degree of disclosure, and therefore the highest level of intuition.

Some Sufis said:

Knowledge of certainty belongs to separation. The eye of certainty belongs to gathering. The truth of certainty belongs to the gathering of gathering.

Domineering: When a seeker or someone at an intermediate stage uses his spiritual states to lord it verbally over people like himself.

It is blameworthy.

This agrees with what we said earlier: people of knowledge do not exercise their power over people. They exercise it over the forces that dominate people.

Unity: The Sufis use this word in a sense different from the ordinary religious meaning of God’s oneness against polytheism.

They call it the unity of the elect.

It means that God makes you one through Himself, sets you apart for Himself, lets you witness this, and makes you absent through Him from everything else you witness.

The ordinary religious meaning of unity as the opposite of polytheism does not appear among the characteristic Sufi meanings of the word. For them, God is absolute existence, and categories such as one and two do not properly apply to Him.

Sufi unity is therefore union.

Singling out: To isolate the unique by removing createdness from it in order to realise the eternal, and to isolate the Eternal by recognising the realities of uniqueness.

Its meaning is more exact than ordinary religious monotheism.

Someone said:

Those who affirm unity are many. Those who truly single out the One among them are few.

It is the final form of unity, completely free of any suspicion of partnership.

Al-Hallaj said:

It is enough for the One that the One be singled out.23

Uniqueness is more exact than simple oneness.

But uniqueness does not prevent union. Union comes only after stripping away, when signs of divinity become clear to hearts once they have been purified of cloudiness.

Spirit contains neither partnership nor multiplicity.

“Singling out” can also mean stripping oneself of forms and states and becoming single in one’s actions.

Here we are dealing only with ethics.

A person’s actions should be for the Real, not for the self—that is vanity—and not for other people—that is flattery.

Nor should he act in hope of compensation.

He should seek no personal gain from what he does.

The undivided concern and undivided secret are the knower’s concern and inner secret once they have been freed from all distractions and devoted completely to watching the Real.

No passing thought cuts across them, and no obstacle prevents attention, approach, nearness, or connection.

The greatest concern is what our noble master identified as:

bringing comfort to people.

This belongs to undivided concern because the knower, absorbed in the Real, gives up his own share for the sake of others.

Conversation: A description of the final state of the utterly truthful.

It resembles revelation, except that it comes without an intermediary.

They even fashioned a hadith for it:

In my community there are people who are spoken to and inspired, and Umar is one of them.

But Umar never claimed sainthood, and he had no such direct conversation.

He belonged to Muhammad’s mission in the field of politics, not religion. He was the man who consolidated and expanded the Islamic state.

That kind of work does not require revelation.

Intimate prayer: The secrets speaking in the clarity that follows remembrance.

It normally comes after remembrance and often takes place at night.

One of al-Junayd’s intimate prayers says:

My God and my Master, do You wish to cut me off from You by joining me to You?

Divine love contains neither cutting off nor joining.

If either occurs to the lover, his ecstasy becomes loss, as we have already explained.

Night converse: Prolonged intimate reproach while secrecy remains intact.

It can also mean the Real addressing the knowers from the world of secrets and the unseen.

Or it can mean spirits alone with the hidden intimacy of their private conversation.

Name: Letters used to point from the act of naming toward the existence of the thing named.

Abu al-Husayn used to illustrate this with the following line:

When a child’s hunger touches his mother, she feeds him with the child’s own name, and the child finds shelter.

Al-Shibli said:

Reality was lost in knowledge, knowledge was lost in the name, and the name was lost in the Essence.

The mother whose child is hungry—and there are many like her today in our country, Iraq—feeds him from the very essence of being.

That essence is his name from childhood.

The child grows hungry and cries out for help, seeking shelter. But he finds no one to protect him except me, and the state stands as a veil between us.

So he dies.

Even as I say this, I seek refuge from saying it—unless the mother is not merely an individual mother, but the mother of a child who has absorbed the secret of existence, allowing her child to become rooted in the Essence.

Childhood then becomes his food.

Childhood itself needs food in order to survive, but the essence of childhood feeds on itself.

This is why I say that the essence of childhood will remain in Iraq without food until the veil is removed and childhood returns, multiplying and reproducing itself through nourishment.

The essence can do without food.

Its individual embodiments cannot.24

Essence: A thing that stands by itself.

Name, description, and attribute are signs pointing toward the Essence.

Nothing has an essence without being named, described, and given attributes.

Veil: Something that comes between the thing being sought and the person seeking it.

Sari al-Saqati used to pray:

My God, whatever else You punish me with, do not punish me with the humiliation of the veil.

Sahl al-Tustari said:

The thickest veil between the servant and God is the claim.

He means claiming to have arrived when one has not arrived.

Or perhaps he meant something else that has not reached us.

Trial: The Real putting the servant’s true state to the test through affliction: what descends on him in the form of suffering, so that the degree of his patience becomes known.

A poet said:

Poor man, the trial is on me—I mean that among all trials, this one is light to me.

One form of trial is illness in the body without panic.

Another is losing something dear, or someone whose loss is painful.

Another is finding oneself in a struggle and remaining firm.

Patience under such trials is praiseworthy.

But patience can also be blameworthy when the affliction consists in people being robbed of their rights, or a person being deprived of the basic necessities of life.

Al-Niffari said:

I am amazed by anyone who finds nothing to eat in his house and does not go out against the people with his sword drawn.

Here patience is blameworthy.

Outrage is required.

Secret: What the Real has hidden and not disclosed to creation.

Sahl al-Tustari said:

The self has a secret which the Real revealed only through Pharaoh’s tongue when he said: “I am your highest lord.”

This is one of al-Tustari’s ecstatic utterances.

The Sufis stand with Pharaoh against Moses because they reject intermediaries.

As for Pharaoh’s words, “I am your highest lord,” this is the secret of the self when it strips itself bare, drinks from the cup of nearness, and unites with the Real, so that the human being becomes divine.

But Shaykh al-Tustari failed to notice that Pharaoh’s claim to lordship does not follow the Sufi pattern.

Pharaoh wanted to make himself a god over people.

The Sufis wanted to become divine for people.

Secret of the secret: What the Real keeps entirely to Himself, beyond even the servant.

Here lies the motive that drives the search for the unknown.

If the secret of the secret were known, knowledge itself would come to an end.

The pact, or pact of the secret: Something the knower commits himself to in his heart, between himself and God: that he will do this or that.

Al-Tirmidhi said:

For thirty years I have made no pact between myself and God Almighty, for fear that He might overturn it and make my own tongue prove me false.

The pact of the heart belongs to the elect.

A spoken pledge belongs to ordinary people.

Here “ordinary people” does not mean the ignorant masses. It means people outside the Sufi path.

Glance: The inward eye noticing what flashes before it as an increase in certainty regarding what it believes of the unseen.

Effacement: The disappearance of something until no trace remains.

If a trace remains, it is blotting out.

Eradication has the same general meaning as effacement, but is more complete.

These are degrees of annihilation.

Al-Shibli said:

I am effaced in what He is…

Meaning:

Nothing comes from anything. Nothing is in me. Nothing comes from me. Everything is from Him, through Him, and for Him.

Sufi effacement is the removal of the attributes of the self.

Some distinguished more carefully between the terms.

Effacement is the annihilation of one’s actions in the action of the Real, so that action proceeds from beyond ordinary reason.

Eradication is the annihilation of one’s very existence in the Essence of the Real.

Blotting out is the annihilation of one’s attributes in the attributes of the Real.

The effacement of gathering is the annihilation of multiplicity in unity.

These are the various degrees in which Sufi annihilation can be understood.

People in our own age sometimes confuse these terms because they have become distant from us—or because we have become distant from them—across many centuries.

So let us put it plainly.

The knower is annihilated in the spirit of the universe, which has been given many names: God, the Creator, the Real, Tao, the Absolute.

All are names for one reality.

This annihilation has two sides.

First, the knower strips away his ordinary qualities, allowing him to become absorbed in the Absolute. He moves through the kingdom of the universe, wandering among its qualities of beauty and kindling his spirit and the energies hidden within it.

Then he emerges from effacement into the second side, ready to act.

The action is his action and, at the same time, the action of others.

It is his because it is carried out through him, by his own decision and choice.

But it is not his alone, because he acts while immersed in something greater.

Suppose, for example, that he joins the poor in confronting the states of the rich.

He acts by a decision of his own self.

But the action does not belong to him alone, because he acts with those around him.

Without them, he would have no action.

Alongside this, the knower experiences happiness as a knowing self spiritualised in the Absolute.

The Absolute is beautiful.

For the Sufis, the world too is beautiful.

As for me, I find the world beautiful when I am alone with it.

I do not find it beautiful when I am among people.

They are being tortured in it.

Trace: A sign left by something.

Someone said:

Whoever is prevented from direct vision finds comfort in the trace.
