But a trace can also be something that must be escaped, when it is the trace of something that should itself be removed.

Al-Khawwas was asked about the unity of the elect and said that it meant turning away from the effects that things leave on their souls.

The trace in which a person deprived of vision finds comfort, on the other hand, means the visible forms and manifestations of existence.

Being and separation: Al-Junayd said of those who had realised unity:

They were without being, and separated without separation.

The meaning is that they are among things as though they were not among them, and apart from things as though they were not apart.

They are among things bodily.

They are apart from them in their secrets.

Someone wrote:

Alone, he wandered lost in the wilderness of unity, and Husayn disappeared in the glory of seeking You.

You appeared to one who affirmed You after his distance, and he was without being—as though You had become him.

Union and separation: Union means the arrival of what was absent.

Some defined it as cutting oneself off from everything except the Real.

It does not mean one physical essence joining another, because that kind of contact belongs only to bodies.

The same is true in human love.

When the Sufi speaks of union, he understands it as the woman who came at the hour of death understood it, not as the ordinary love poet understands it.

We have already discussed this.

Union and separation overlap.

Anyone who thinks he has arrived should know that he has already separated.

As one poet said:

No union and no separation, no despair and no hope.

Al-Jawahiri touched the same meaning when he wrote of Zahle in Lebanon:

Love is Zahle-like: no joining, no turning away, no withholding, no giving.

There is nothing about Zahle itself that makes it so, nor did the poet deliberately create this meaning.

The Merciful simply overflowed through his tongue.

Our Sufis used separation rather than abandonment, because abandonment belongs to the vocabulary of ordinary love poetry.

Adorning oneself: Taking on the speech of the sincere and displaying their actions outwardly.

Manifestation: What is disclosed to hearts from the lights of the unseen.

It has three forms:

manifestation of the Essence, manifestation of the attributes of the Essence, and manifestation of the judgment of the Essence.

The first is disclosure and vision.

The second is the place of light.

When divine power manifests itself to the knower, he fears no one else.

And when he fears no one, his own action becomes something no one need fear.

At this level manifestation also brings self-sufficiency, because the knower needs no one else.

The manifestation of the judgment of the Essence belongs to the next world.

Manifestation through attributes is a state descending on the knower through the attributes that are the divine names.

These names also become descriptions of the person receiving the manifestation.

If manifestation comes through the name the Merciful, mercy becomes one of his attributes.

If it comes through the Generous, he becomes generous.

If it comes through the Powerful, he possesses power.

The Beautiful Names are therefore attributes shared, in this sense, by the One who manifests and the person to whom He manifests.

Ahmad al-Rifaʿi said that when the servant becomes firmly established in the states, he becomes an attribute of the Real and nothing can defeat him.

He cited a sacred saying:

O son of Adam, obey Me and I will obey you. I will make you able to say to a thing, “Be,” and it will be.

Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri said:

He manifested Himself to His creation through His creation, and hid Himself from His creation through His creation.

Here manifestation is understood through things in their relations with one another.

Creation is His image and the field of His action.

At the same time, creation is His veil.

Strictly speaking, He appears and acts only through their appearance and action.

Our Sufis knew this just as the philosophers did.

But the higher human being does not accept nature exactly as it is.

He rebuilds it so that it serves needs greater than those supplied by nature alone.

Sufism does not explain nature.

It changes it.

Emptying oneself: Turning away from the things that distract a person from the Real.

This is also a Buddhist idea.

It is usually linked to withdrawal.

What must be left behind are bodily demands beyond natural need, together with the self’s desire for status, power, and fame.

Everlasting: Permanent and unchanging.

Al-Shibli said:

My time in You has become everlasting, and it is everlasting.

Al-Sarraj al-Tusi comments that al-Shibli is describing the quality of his secret, not the quality of his ordinary attributes.

Attributes change.

The secret endures.

Subtle insight: Something that flashes before understanding and gleams in the mind, but is too fine in meaning for language to contain.

Overwhelming seizure: A force that descends on the mind and carries it away through the strength of its domination.

Freedom: A sign of the final fulfilment of servanthood to God.

It means that nothing in creation owns you.

You are free when you are a servant of God.

Bishr al-Hafi said:

God created you free, so remain as He created you. Do not perform for your family when you are at home or for your companions when you travel. Work for God and leave people alone.

Al-Junayd said:

The final station of the knower is freedom.

Someone else said:

A servant cannot truly be a servant while still enslaved by anything other than God.

Servanthood to God is therefore freedom among people.

Freedom also means the knower becoming free of his own self.

Shuʿayb Abu Madyan pointed to this when he said:

No one reaches pure freedom while anything of himself still remains.

Becoming free of the self means becoming free of its excessive claims on life and wealth.

What a person owns also owns him, as the Sufis used to say.

His desires enslave him.

Abu al-Atahiya wrote:

I obeyed my desires, and they enslaved me.

They claimed that al-Hallaj recited this while crucified.

Hardly.

Desire was never capable of enslaving him.

Freedom, as al-Junayd said, is the knower’s station at the final stages.

It is the highest goal of travelling the path.

Rust: The corrosion that settles on hearts.

Someone said that hearts can be veiled in four ways.

Then he listed six.

There is sealing and imprinting, which belong to the hearts of unbelievers.

There is rust and hardness, which belong to hypocrites.

And there is tarnish and covering, which belong to believers.

Six, not four.

Clouding: A film or haze.

A hadith says:

A clouding comes over my heart, and I ask God’s forgiveness and repent to Him a hundred times each day.

The saying does not appear in the major primary collections, but it is old. It appears in Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam’s Gharib al-Hadith.

The Sufis took hold of it. Al-Sarraj al-Tusi included it.

They explained the clouding by comparing it to a mirror breathed upon by someone looking into it. Its brightness briefly fades, then returns.

Intermediaries: Things standing between the servant and his Lord among the causes of this world and the next.

There are three kinds:

intermediaries in constant communication, connected intermediaries, and disconnected intermediaries.

The first are sudden visitations from the Real.

The second are acts of worship.

The third are the shares of the self.

The outward face of possibilities: The Real manifesting through the individual forms and attributes of possible things.

The idea of “possible things” comes from Ibn Sina. It means things that may either exist or not exist.

Its opposite is the impossible, which cannot exist, and necessary existence, which is absolute existence.

But when all the conditions required for a possible thing come together, its existence becomes necessary.

Plant a seed in suitable soil and a suitable climate, and its development into a tree becomes necessary.

The outward face of existence: The manifestations of the divine names, where unity is real and difference is relative.

This belongs to the philosophy of the unity of being.

Existence is truly one.

Existing things differ in their forms, not in their underlying essence.

The outward face of knowledge: The individual realities of possible things.

That is, the actual existing things whose forms are reflected in the human mind, producing knowledge of their outward appearance.

Knowing their inner reality requires inward knowledge.

Worship: Turning toward God through ritual acts. Its place is the body.

Servanthood: Acknowledging His lordship. Its place is the spirit.

Utter servanthood: The most hidden secret.

Perhaps they separated this last category because it returns to a relation of equality.

Unveiling: Ahmad al-Rifaʿi defined it as:

A power which, by its special nature, draws the light of an eye or inner sight toward the overflowing unseen. Its light joins that unseen as a ray joins clear glass when the glass faces the source of light. The light then rebounds and is reflected onto the purity of the heart. From there it rises, shining, into the world of the intellect and joins it through an immaterial connection whose effect is to pour the light of the intellect back onto the field of the heart. The light of the intellect then shines upon the pupil of the inner secret, and the person sees what ordinary eyes cannot locate and ordinary understanding cannot conceive.

This is a good description of the power of intuition.

I apologise to specialists in the art.

This is the kind of passage one is meant to taste and absorb, not explain.

But I am defining terms here, so I have no choice.

Fluctuation and settledness: Two stages in the knower’s path.

In the first, his qualities are unstable and change according to the different states passing through him.

He then rises from fluctuation to settledness.

Here realities are disclosed to him and become firmly established.

Of course, nothing in a human being can ever be absolutely fixed. Human beings continue to change.

What is meant is that a truth once disclosed to him never again disappears or grows weaker. It only deepens.

Someone still in fluctuation may contradict himself when the qualities of his ordinary self reappear. He remains exposed to change and forgetting.

Settledness belongs with witnessing.

Taste: In ordinary usage, a faculty that recognises subtle qualities of speech and delicate forms of beauty.

Among the Sufis, it is a light of knowledge cast by the Real, through manifestation, into the hearts of His friends. By it they distinguish truth from falsehood.

It is the first manifestation.

It belongs to people of sudden visitations.

But taste is also a general means of understanding and one of the powers of intuition.

The olive: A symbol of the self when it is ready to ignite with the light of holiness because of the strength of its oil.

The oil represents its original preparedness.

Qahwāʾiyya: The Real addressing a person directly, face-to-face, in the imaginal world.

Perhaps the term was formed from words relating to the mouth and its opening.

Meeting-place of opposites: Absolute identity: the presence in which the furthest extremes embrace and opposites meet beneath a single identity.

Meeting-place of the two seas: The presence of “two bow-lengths,” in which the two seas of necessity and possibility meet.

“Two bow-lengths” means the nearness of the meeting.

The meeting is between possibility and necessity.

It is also defined as the presence in which existence is gathered together through the meeting of divine names and cosmic realities.

Veiling and manifestation: Al-Junayd said:

It is discipline, refinement, and dissolution.

Discipline belongs to veiling and is for ordinary people.

Refinement belongs to the elect and is manifestation.

Dissolution belongs to the saints and is witnessing.

Veiling draws the saints back out of the gathering of gathering so that people can benefit from them.

If they remained permanently there, they would be cut off from creation.

The knower therefore has times for himself and times for people.

His time for himself is the gathering of gathering.

His time for people is separation.

Helper: The Pole when people turn to him for help.

He is not called the Helper at other times.

From this we can understand the function of the Helper as action taken to confront some difficulty that has fallen on an individual or a group.

The present moment: The state in which the Sufi is present in his heart with God.

A saying attributed to the Prophet runs:

I have a moment with God in which neither an angel brought near nor a prophet sent with a message has room to enter.

The present moment is now.

It is a word suspended between two non-existent things: the past and the future.

The past has gone.

The future has not yet arrived.

The faqir is the child of his moment.

This concentrates the Sufi’s attention on the present, turning him away from dwelling on the past or looking toward the future.

But this should be understood only as a state of attention.

A human being cannot truly cut himself off from the past.

He is the child of his past, not merely the child of the present moment.

His existence arose in the past, whose time is not fundamentally separate from the time of the present. Moments of time and what accompanies them are distinct, as Aristotle counted them, but they form a sequence.

As for thinking about the future, sometimes we do and sometimes we do not.

But removing the future entirely from human thought also removes one of the motives for action.

That is a negative thing.

Ibn Arabi defined the present moment as:

Your state in the time of the present state.

That is, a passing state.

The best definition, to my mind, is the one given by someone who said:

Your moment is whatever has mastery over you in this instant.

The exalted letters: The hidden affairs of the Essence concealed in the unseen of the unseen, like the tree hidden in the seed.

Ibn Arabi wrote:

We were exalted letters, never spoken, suspended on the summits of the highest peaks.

The self-reproaching soul: The soul illuminated enough by the light of the heart to wake from the sleep of heedlessness.

Whenever it commits a wrong through the darkness built into its nature, it begins to blame itself.

What the Sufis called the self-reproaching soul is what people today call the conscience or the superego.

Awe and intimacy: Two states higher than contraction and expansion.

Awe requires absence.

Intimacy requires sobriety and waking awareness.

Awe prevents intimacy.

The red ruby: The universal soul, whose light is mixed with the darkness that comes from attachment to the body.

The separate intellect, by contrast, is pure light.

For the Sufis, the individual soul is the site of blameworthy qualities and one of the veils covering the intellect.

The universal soul is a mixture of the light of absolute existence and the darkness of particular existence, which in this relation is the body.

Witnessing: Presence, sometimes in the form of watchfulness and sometimes in the form of direct vision.

The unity of witnessing means creation merging into the Real until no distinction is experienced between them.

It can sometimes approach what has been called the unity of the existent, an idea I reject because things have their own independence and distinction from absolute existence.

The unity of the existent means that nothing truly exists except God, while all other beings are illusions and shadows.

This comes close to the subjective idealism of some modern European philosophers.

A few Sufis expressed ideas like this.

But most of them held to the unity of being, not the unity of the existent.

That means absolute existence multiplying itself through existing things.

Those things become many and distinct and acquire an existence independent from absolute existence, even though they continue to draw existence from it.

In nature, the relationship resembles that between a seed and a tree.

The seed is the original existence.

The tree derives from it.

Yet the tree becomes independent.

A tree in its essence is not the same thing as a seed in its essence.

Those who believe in the unity of the existent make the tree the seed and the seed the tree.

Dialectical logic allows this in one sense: the tree is absent in the seed and the seed is absent in the tree.

But this does not abolish their separation in essence.

If we move from this example to the relation between the Real and creation, we see the Real flowing through existing things or manifesting Himself in them.

Those manifestations take different forms.

Our senses testify to those differences.

The things are therefore not identical with the Real.

For this reason, subjective idealism never became widespread among the Sufis.

References to it appear only occasionally, usually in loose, passing remarks or in attempts to complete an unfinished expression.

Overpowering state: Ecstasy that continues without interruption.

Ecstasy may die away quickly.

When it lasts and continues, it becomes an overpowering state.

Explanation of Some Phrases and Expressions

Drawing the spirits: Abu Saʿid al-Kharraz said:

God drew the spirits of His friends toward Himself and gave them pleasure in remembering Him—

he should have said delighted them, because pleasure is bodily—

and in reaching nearness to Him. He hastened to give their bodies pleasure in everything, so that their bodies live the life of animals while their spirits live the life of those close to the divine.

His phrase “He hastened to give their bodies pleasure” is a bad one.

The bodies of the knowers do not take pleasure.

Their spirits are what rejoice.

My sea has no shore: A phrase of al-Shibli’s, spoken during one of his gatherings:

Your moments are cut off. My moment has no two ends, and my sea has no shore.

He means that the state God has given him has neither end nor interruption.

A person of the heart: Someone unable to express in eloquent speech the knowledge gathered in his heart.

Al-Junayd used to say:

The people of Khurasan are people of hearts.

He meant the Sufis of Khurasan.

They could not express themselves fluently in Arabic, so their hearts spoke instead of their tongues.

A person of a state: Someone connected to a particular state, such as love, fear, hope, or longing.

A person of a station: Someone who has acquired a particular lasting station, such as scrupulousness, asceticism, patience, or opposition.

Without a self: To say that someone is “without a self” means that the ordinary qualities of the self no longer appear in him.

These include anger, harshness, pride, greed, craving, and envy.

A person of allusion: Someone whose speech contains subtle meanings and indirect signs.

I without I: Said by someone who has given up ownership of his actions within the very act of doing them.

That is, he does not act for himself.

It also describes someone who has given up his personal claims.

And it can mean surrendering the self to the beloved.

A poet wrote:

O desire of every desirer, You took me through You away from me.

That is:

You stripped me of my “I.”

The Taoists also speak of giving up ownership of action within action.

The sage acts, then withdraws.

Ranks of Those Who Enter the Path

Seeker: Defined above.

Intermediate: Someone who has travelled some distance as a seeker and acquired states, but has not yet acquired stations.

Traveller: Someone who has arrived after passing through the stages of seeker and intermediate.

Travellers themselves have different levels and ranks according to their capacities.

Knower: The traveller at the highest level.

He is also the sought one.

Pole: The highest knower, around whom the movement of creation comes to revolve.

He is called the Helper when people turn to him for help.

Poleship is the rank of the Pole.

I use the term Sufism of the Poles to distinguish this from ordinary Sufism practised by the general mass of Sufis and their lesser figures.

As we have already seen, the function of the Helper means action by the Pole to solve a difficulty facing an individual or a group.

Faqir: The common name for a Sufi, because poverty is the pattern of his personality once he has freed himself from servitude to money and ownership.

Its plural is faqirs, or people of poverty.

People of the Real: The Sufis’ name for themselves.

The aspiring Sufi and the Sufi: Usually two names for the same thing.

Some, however, treat them as two stages: first the aspiring Sufi, then the Sufi, taking this from the grammatical form of the Arabic word, which can suggest gradually becoming something.

Guide of the path: Someone who teaches seekers the road into Sufism—that is, someone who brings them into the path.

Assessment

There has been a great deal of disagreement over where the word Sufism comes from. The most common view derives it from ṣūf, wool. Wool was what poor people and ascetics wore, provided it was not finely woven. Coarse wool was the norm. Fine wool, by contrast, was sought after by the rich, by rulers, and by people accustomed to comfort. Ordinary wool was rough and crude. Such people found no pleasure in wearing it and preferred silk, linen, and cotton.

Islam forbade men to wear silk, and Umar ibn al-Khattab forbade his governors to wear linen, leaving them wool and cotton. Even today, our peasants wear a rough woollen cloth called the bisht. Iraqis have a saying about the man in the bisht, used for the poor and powerless person who gets into a dispute with someone who has authority—a merchant, a soldier, an official, or an intellectual.

It is also possible that the word Sufi is related to the Arabic ṣūfiyā, carrying the sense of a seer, revealer, or diviner. The word is native to the Semitic languages; perhaps the Greek sophia is related to it.

But I am more inclined to connect Sufism with wool, because Sufism began as a social movement founded on asceticism and opposition to the feudal way of life of state officials and the property-owning classes. It did not begin as an intellectual movement. Philosophy entered it later.

Modern researchers who have tried to get away from wool and search for some other origin with more philosophical or cultural associations are really expressing the intellectual’s dislike of wool—or embarrassment at having to wear it.

The history of Sufism today suffers from outside interventions that have tried to appropriate it for culture in the narrow sense. New books appear, or old books are edited and republished, financed by rich people and governments, while their authors and editors bask in the comforts of both worlds.

Worse still are groups who claim family descent from the great communalist Sufi masters, or claim to follow their path, then use their names to grow rich at the expense of hungry people. Aristocratic families are formed around a name while knowing nothing of what the name once stood for.

Sufism, in both its social and philosophical forms, came to an end with Abd al-Karim al-Jili, who died in 832 AH. After him came books of biographies that recorded the tradition, explained it, or repeated what its great masters had written and said during the Islamic age, which in this sense does not extend beyond the generation of the last great master, Abd al-Karim.

No one has the right to claim membership in the path when both of its real paths have disappeared.

We have returned to Sufism as part of our return to the heritage. We are trying to revive and develop it by joining it to social Marxism and enriching it with the Chinese form of Sufism known as Taoism.

Our own social Sufism and Taoism together provide the foundation for a bottom-up communism, a grassroots communism, to be built on the ruins of top-down communism—the communism of bourgeois Marxists.

In the final orbit devoted to Sufism, we put forward a project for a Communalist Association of Iraq. It begins from social Sufism and Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani’s principle of “bringing comfort to the people,” together with the Taoist project of the Great Society. It joins these to Marxist organisation and draws inspiration from the Paris Commune, the Qarmatians of Iraq, the movement of Jesus, Mazdak, and Abu Dharr al-Ghifari.

Our writers today endlessly repeat the language of “failure,” translated from the Latin and Germanic languages.

Taoism failed. Jesus failed. The philosophers of Islam failed. The Sufis failed. Marxism failed. Guevara failed. The October Revolution failed. The Bolsheviks failed. Chinese communism failed.

The only people who succeeded, apparently, are our writers and their own little projects—projects isolated from one another and at war with one another over who owns the patent.

Every researcher now plants himself at the centre of life and history, master of the whole spectacle, looking down on the dead: all of them failures. Civilisations failed. The people who made them failed. Their martyrs failed. History itself withdrew.

Only the successful researcher remained.

Perhaps Abu Yazid al-Bistami foresaw this farce in one of his visions.

A man once told him that he had spent thirty years in worship and had still not arrived.

Bistami explained to him that arrival would not come through worship. He should go out dressed exactly as he was, mount a donkey, carry walnuts through the marketplace, and let the children follow behind him, whistling and clapping.

Then he would become a Sufi master.

Yes.

When souls are great, bodies grow weary in pursuing their aims.

And the reverse is also true.

Sufism is a social culture with a communalist root. It inhabits a large soul before which the prestige of the ruler and his state collapses, along with the prestige of money and its owners. Anxiety over reputation, fame, success, and intellectual patents disappears.

Cultural identity is then realised by sitting with the poor and helping them clean the lice from their clothes when the unsuccessful cosmopolitan intellectual cannot even provide them with soap—because, like them, he owns nothing.

Sufism began with Ibrahim ibn Adham.

Before him there were people who did not belong to the Sufi path but carried some of its concerns. They were, so to speak, its forerunners. They helped draw a line within Islamic culture that identified itself with ordinary people and stood in conflict with the state.

They included theologians, jurists, and religious scholars whose consciences were communalist and fiercely independent. They hated the state and its masters and stood with its victims.

The founders of speculative theology were all killed in the struggle against Umayyad despotism. The overwhelming majority of the jurists of the first Islamic century sided with the opposition. They carried out their role as defenders of rights, not as professional men of religion.

The Umayyads had little on their side except poets.

This explains why the Sufi biographical collections, and similar books, include lives of people who lived before Sufism existed. They were counted among the Sufis even though they were not actually Sufis. It is more accurate to call them forerunners.

This is why Sufi books quote them as though they were among the tradition’s own teachers.

Among them were Amir al-Anbari, whom the biographical works describe as a Sufi even though he was one of the generation after the Companions and a student of Salman al-Farisi; Malik ibn Dinar; Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak; Sufyan al-Thawri; Sufyan ibn Uyayna; Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani; Tawus al-Yamani; Dawud al-Ta’i; Ibn al-Sammak al-Kufi; and others like them.

They were ascetics, opponents of power, and people deeply concerned for others.

But they were not Sufis.

Al-Qushayri says in his Epistle that the name Sufi first appeared in the third Islamic century. Yet the real beginning should be placed with Ibrahim ibn Adham in the middle of the second century. He was the first to use recognisably Sufi terminology, speak in the language of the tradition, and express its basic principles.

We have already seen that he came from Balkh, in what is now Afghanistan, close to China. That invites us to imagine that he may have encountered something of Taoism.

But, as I have said, this is only an idea. We have no evidence that allows us to go further.

We can, however, imagine oral transmission. Ibn Adham may have heard about the Taoists and their ideas from Chinese sages who were known in Central Asia before Islam.

Central Asia lay within China’s political and cultural sphere to such an extent that when al-Tabari describes Qutayba’s arrival at Kashgar, the capital of East Turkestan, he gives the passage the heading:

“Qutayba’s Arrival in the Land of China.”

Whatever the case, Sufism arose naturally from the growth of tendencies that already contained its basic principles, even though they had not yet come together in a distinct language of their own.

It did not appear in a vacuum.

Sufism continued along its two main lines through a history of roughly six centuries.

The social form came first. That was the path of its “founder,” Ibn Adham.

Philosophical Sufism began with Abu Yazid al-Bistami, though it did not become a fully distinct school until Ibn Arabi in the sixth Islamic century.

Bistami’s philosophy is contained in his ecstatic sayings. Those sayings broke down the walls of inherited belief and created a way of thinking outside traditional religious frameworks.

With them, Bistami shocked the Islamic mind out of its skull and sent it soaring into an immense open space where it could move with almost complete freedom.

He struck directly at the habit of thinking through sacred things.

Sacred objects and ideas fell from their pedestal in his speech and became ordinary things he could play with according to wherever the current of his thought carried him.

Once he had brought prophetic sacredness down to size, he did not stop for long before divinity itself.

His wild ascent continued until he collided with the Throne.

Either he brought the Throne down to earth or climbed onto it himself, depending on whether his vision happened to be rising or descending.

He removed the barrier between earth and heaven by placing the human being and the Lord on equal terms.

Philosophical Sufism denies that the spirit was created. It must therefore also deny slavery as the proper relation between Creator and created.

Bistami rejected it in the ecstatic saying in which he addressed God:

“The whole world is my slave except You.”

But he did not erase God from existence.

He still needed a cosmic spirit to serve as a Buraq carrying him upward through the higher kingdom, freeing him from the slavery of earthly sensation.

He did not deprive God of action. Instead, he made the divine act through his own humanity.

The Real acts through the human being—but not through just any human being.

It needs a human being capable of breaking through the necessities imposed by nature and reshaping them through reason, thereby matching the process of creation itself, which produced nature as this mixture of perfection and imperfection.

Humanity is one essence, but it takes form in different individuals. Not every individual human being can do what another can do.

When we speak of a human being becoming divine, we do not mean just anyone.

That stage requires certain conditions, reached by a particular person through labour and struggle.

Everyone struggles, but toward different ends.

If someone works to become a blacksmith or carpenter, he reaches that goal, while another person exactly like him may be incapable of it. Becoming a blacksmith or carpenter requires time, effort, and skill that another person may not possess.

The person who labours toward divinity can also reach his goal—a goal the blacksmith and carpenter will not reach.

The division of labour does not exist in economics alone. It applies to every part of life.

What Bistami attained cannot be reached by someone else except under the same conditions that carried him to his goal.25

Just as people benefit from the labour of the blacksmith and carpenter, they benefit from the labour of Bistami and others in the same profession.

Every profession benefits people in its own way, through its own methods, levels, stages, and degrees, depending on the field in which it operates and the kind of expertise it requires.

Human liberation from slavery passes through two stages.

The first is to replace slavery to other human beings with servitude to God, following the Islamic-Christian principle:

Be the servant of the Lord, not the servant of creation.

Even this liberation has not yet been completed.

In most of the world, human beings are still slaves to other human beings.

Religious corruption makes matters worse by combining servitude to God with servitude to people, directly contradicting the Islamic-Christian principle.

This is why Islamic thinkers repeatedly insisted on distinguishing the two kinds of servitude and making servitude to God conditional on freedom from servitude to human beings.

The Sufis made this effort more consistently than anyone else.

Perhaps this explains why they so often called a human being an abd, a servant, and much less often a believer.

Servant is a description shared by all people, regardless of religion or faith. It makes them equal before God and requires that they be slaves to no one else.

It seems that some of the great masters became impatient, or simply grew tired of waiting for humanity to complete its liberation from human slavery before moving on to the end of servitude to God.

Perhaps Bistami’s declaration came out of that impatience.

That is his own affair.

Once he had freed himself from slavery to others, broken free from the outside powers that ruled him, and become master of himself, he turned toward the final chain limiting his sense of complete sovereignty.

He abolished his servitude to God.

Later masters in the atheistic current of Sufism followed the same decision. They declared:

“The spirit never fell beneath the humiliation of ‘Be.’”

That is: the human spirit is not created.

And if it is not created, it is not the slave of a creator.

In the older Arab language, createdness itself carried an implication of subjection, while servitude to God placed a chain around the human essence.

Some Sufis therefore objected even to being called Abd Allah, servant of God.

The expression became common in Islam as a way of addressing a stranger whose name you did not know: “O Abd Allah”—in other words, “you there.”

We are still a very long way from freeing human beings from slavery to one another.

That liberation must come before liberation from servitude to God.

But this does not mean Bistami failed at this stage.

He attained it for himself and created a model that others after him could struggle toward.

Humanity’s rescuers are always early.

They sleep lightly.

Bistami is the master of philosophical Sufism.

The closest students to him were Abu Bakr al-Shibli and then al-Hallaj: Shibli through ecstatic utterance, and Hallaj through both ecstatic utterance and writing.

Shibli combined intellectual Sufism with the Sufism of passionate love. As we have suggested, he was in love with a human woman whose name he never revealed.

Hallaj loved without attaching that love to one identifiable human beloved. He was also an intellectual Sufi and a social-communalist Sufi.

He was a plant watered by all three rivers.

Intellectual Sufism developed slowly through al-Makki in The Nourishment of Hearts, al-Sarraj al-Tusi in The Book of Flashes, and al-Kalabadhi in The Doctrine of the Sufis, before reaching its summit in Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi, the greatest philosopher of Sufism.

By coincidence or otherwise, he lived at the same time as the great master of passionate Sufism, Umar ibn al-Farid.

Ibn Arabi was a philosopher and should be counted among the philosophers of Islam. His philosophical theories, above all the unity of being, should be studied as achievements of Islamic philosophy.

The martyred scholar should really have discussed him in the philosophy section of Materialist Tendencies, not under Sufism.

Had I ever met him—may God sanctify his secret—I would have pointed this out.

With Ibn Arabi, principles first established by earlier Sufis reached maturity. They took settled form in his work and continued after him in Ibn Sabʿin and Abd al-Karim al-Jili.

We have discussed them in detail throughout these orbits. Here they are in brief:

  1. All religions stand on equal ground with respect to truth. Religions and atheism do too, as do revealed religions and pagan religions. No party has the right to monopolise truth. It follows that one dominant religion must no longer persecute or suppress another, and that the tide of religious warfare and conflict must be stopped.

  2. Sainthood is placed on a level with prophecy. Alongside the Seal of the Prophets appears the idea of the Seal of the Saints, together with an impulse to proclaim the great Sufi master himself a prophet—an impulse blocked by the saying, “There is no prophet after me.”

  3. The walls of doctrine are broken down so that the mind can escape its skull and think without restraints. To complete this liberation of thought, Sufism took another step and broke through the laws of formal logic as well. This was done in favour of intuition and dialectics. The Sufis and Taoists share in the ancestry of dialectical logic, to which the Greek philosopher Heraclitus also made a major contribution.

    Intuition and dialectics made possible al-Shirazi’s philosophical revolution. He was both philosopher and illuminationist, and it was through illumination that this method reached him. It carried him beyond the walls of formal logic and allowed him to see the movement of substance and the unity of opposites that drives that movement. Had Shirazi remained inside Aristotelian logic, he would have remained just another commentator on Aristotle.

  4. The principle of happiness in both worlds is rejected, at least for the great Sufi master. Ibn Arabi was less explicit on this point than the masters of social Sufism. He rejected eternal torment in hell, either interpreting it as a special form of pleasure experienced by the people of the Fire, or as punishment lasting only as long as their sins require before turning into pleasure. He also made the pleasures of paradise spiritual rather than material. Shirazi reports him as saying that life continues and never stops, a position that leads toward denial of a final resurrection.

These foundations of philosophical Sufism were inherited by Ibn Sabʿin in the generation immediately after Ibn Arabi.

He reproduced them in his books and letters and helped spread them more widely.

Like Ibn Arabi, Ibn Sabʿin was a believer in the unity of being, a dialectical thinker, a deist, and a universalist in matters of belief.

He left behind a group named after him. They treated religious rituals lightly, though without falling into moral libertinism.

A hundred years later came Abd al-Karim al-Jili, who renewed Ibn Arabi’s whole system in all its elements and became the last great master in the line of philosophical Sufism.

One thing has always puzzled me.

Why do the great biographical dictionaries and collections of Sufi lives ignore this magnificent figure?

Al-Sha’rani gives him no biography. Nor do Ibn al-Mulaqqin, al-Sakhawi, Ibn al-Imad, or al-Munawi.

Did they simply not know him?

Or did they seek refuge in God from him and leave him in the dark?

I cannot say for certain, especially because al-Munawi embraced Hallaj and defended him—and Hallaj was more dangerous than Jili to states and social systems, while being just as dangerous to established religions.

Social Sufism was a movement of struggle within the field of Asian communalism.

Its companions there were the Taoist philosophers and Jesus.

I know of no equivalent companion in the other great civilisations of the East.

Take India, for example. I looked through its philosophy and then closed the book again. I found religion, and little else.

The Hungarian communist Lukács was entitled to lament its passivity and submissiveness, and to see the same tendency behind both the Nobel Prize awarded to Tagore, the poet who admired ancient Indian wisdom, and Britain’s conquest of India.

The ancient Semites and Egyptians did touch on a form of struggle between communalism on one side and slavery and feudalism on the other. But their cultures did not rise to the point of fully grasping that struggle and creating a wisdom that embraced it, together with sages who would fight openly against the state and the rich in defence of people’s rights.

The idea of people is a common thread between Sufism and Taoism.

The Taoist word is ren.

The Sufis gave the Arabic word khalq—creation, or people—its social meaning. Through them it passed into the languages of Muslim peoples.

So we find expressions such as Afghani Khalq, meaning the Afghan people; Khalq Bank, the People’s Bank; and Khalq Party, the People’s Party.

In Taoist usage, ren combines with min to mean the people, while ren on its own refers to the human being and to humanity.

The Sufis also used words such as the common people and ordinary people.

They rejected the habit of treating these expressions as synonyms for the mob.

They made a distinction.

The ordinary people are those whose hearts are sound, whose conduct is upright, and whose character is good.

If those qualities are absent, then we are dealing with the mob, not the common people.

Once we understand this difference, a number of things that used to seem confused become clearer.

We often hear that “the common people” fight philosophy, persecute philosophers, and rise up at the command of religious authorities against heretics.

In reality, ordinary people respect an honest and modest intellectual.

It is the mob that persecutes.

Every society and every social group contains a mob that can be moved by religious men—or anyone else—for purposes of their own.

A religious mob existed during the Islamic period, and religious authorities used it against thinkers. But the field was never completely open to them because they did not themselves control the state. They had to wait for moments when the state looked the other way before harassing people they accused of heresy.

Ordinary people, on the other hand, normally respond only to calls for jihad against a foreign enemy.

That is the one point on which they may join religious authorities and the state.

The ordinary people I knew in Iraq still had the same attitude toward intellectuals.

They called the intellectual an arifa, “a knowing one,” in a particular familiar tone.

If they sensed that he cared about them and was interested in their affairs, they approached him, asked him questions, and sought his advice.

If a mullah then pronounced him a heretic or something similar, they hesitated. They found excuses for him. They tried to explain him away.

The social struggle of the Sufis was directed toward lifting oppression from people and securing the means of life for them.

At first glance, some of their language about trust in God, asceticism, and patience may appear contradictory.

The contradiction disappears once we understand what they meant by those words and distinguish their meaning from the religious meaning given to them by professional religious authorities.

Religious authorities demand trust, asceticism, and patience from ordinary people.

And religious culture constantly distinguishes between elite and commoner, ruler and ruled, owner and deprived.

This merges easily with the corruption that infects clerical institutions in every religion.

The burden of religious obligations is thrown onto the people and lifted from the rulers and wealthy who form the clergy’s own social circle.

Most religious authorities are not ascetics.

The public display of religion is itself lavish. It shines with decoration, luxury, and ornament.

This produces real crimes against humanity.

Look at the vast amounts spent by Iraqis and Iranians on shrines belonging to all kinds of figures, major and minor, some whose graves are known and others whose association with a site is doubtful.

The waste reaches almost unimaginable levels while the Iranian and Iraqi peoples endure severe crises of daily life, reaching famine in Iraq and crushing poverty in Iran.

The old Muslim social fighters rejected this.

They accused those responsible of violating both justice and religious law.

Religious authorities have no evidence in scripture, prophetic practice, or the traditions of the Imams permitting them to transfer the rights of the poor to shrines.

They are simply following a pattern found among clerical establishments in every religion.

European churches and Buddhist and Hindu temples are no different in this respect from Islamic mosques and shrines, especially Shiite ones.

This is religion everywhere, in every period, across religions and civilisations.

So when religious circles speak of asceticism and trust in God, the message is directed almost entirely at the poor.

Among social fighters and advocates of justice, the equation is reversed.

Very early in Islamic history, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz refused to renew the columns of the Umayyad Mosque because the poor had a greater right to the money than the columns did.

The same principle was maintained by religious scholars, theologians, and jurists whom we have treated as forerunners of Sufism.

We have already discussed Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, a wealthy man who distributed everything beyond his own needs among the poor and refused to spend money on building mosques.

Sufyan al-Thawri spoke painfully of people who erected lavish and decorated buildings, whether mosque or palace.

Al-Ghazali rejected the building of mosques while poor people remained in need of money, as he says in Disclosure and Clarification.

Al-Sha’rani’s Warning to the Deluded contains a great deal of material along the same lines.

Opposition was therefore not confined to palaces.

It extended to mosques and shrines whenever poor people existed who had a greater need for the money.26

Hunger occupied a central place in Sufi concern.

They made it the mother of all problems, and they considered relieving it better than any religious or worldly act.

They did not postpone it to the next world.

The Sufi heart was pressed constantly against the daily sight of hungry people.

The Sufi finds happiness in feeding someone who is hungry: in creating a material, physical happiness for a deprived human being.

Their awareness of popular hunger produced their uncompromising opposition to both the state and the wealthy, because they held these two groups responsible for hunger.

This followed from the position of the state in Asian society.

The state was the effective owner of social wealth. It controlled that wealth, distributed it to a minority, and withheld it from the majority.

The Sufis could see with their own eyes what the state did with money: what it spent on palaces, what it poured into pleasures, and the astonishing channels of waste it opened—waste so extreme that it fell under the legal concept of reckless incompetence for which a person could be denied control of his own property.

The Sufis and the religious scholars close to them therefore fought their class struggle first and foremost against the state.

They cursed it.

They regarded it as pure contamination, something that could not be approached safely.

Whoever touched it became polluted, lost his heart, and turned into one of the human devils.

Their attack on the rich came from the same battlefield of class conflict.

Their opposition to wealth follows the same path as the sages who preceded them: the Taoists, Jesus, and Mazdak among the Persians.

That opposition rests on two arguments.

The first is that concentration of wealth in the hands of a small group necessarily deprives the majority.

As Fakhr al-Din al-Razi observed in his Quranic commentary, the existence of surplus wealth in one person’s hands corresponds to the deprivation of someone else, because wealth is limited. If it is concentrated in a few hands, it cannot reach everyone.

Today some people try to disprove this theory by pointing to the West, where some rich people possess fortunes once enjoyed only by emperors and sultans, while at the same time broad sections of the population enjoy a reasonable standard of living.

But this is an exceptional condition.

The West takes possession of the wealth of the whole world and pumps it into its own countries.

Because the accumulation is so enormous, what the rich take for themselves does not prevent some part of it from reaching the people—not all the people, but a wider section of them.

I once discussed this with a British leftist.

I told him:

“We could start the revolution in Europe ourselves.”

He asked:

“How?”

I said:

“Cut off the oil. Withdraw our money from your banks. Close our markets to your products. Then the capitalists will no longer be able to bribe a large section of the people into keeping quiet.”

He accepted the argument in theory.

But he replied:

“Then the capitalists would turn into the kind of tyrants you have in your countries and drown the people in blood.”

However much resources increase through industrial development, concentration of wealth in a few hands still reduces the share that reaches the people and prevents sufficient resources from being available to meet their needs.

The second reason Sufis and Eastern thinkers in general opposed wealth is that wealth leads to luxury, and luxury corrupts the human being.

Once a person possesses more money than he needs, the range of his appetites expands.

An animal impulse grows inside him, tightening the grip of selfishness and excessive self-concern, blocking his awareness of other people’s interests, rights, and feelings, and drowning him in pleasure-seeking.

This disfigures the human essence.

Through reason, human beings became able to reorganise the demands of nature and restrict them to what is necessary, creating space for a spiritual development that nature itself does not care about.

From nature’s point of view, a human being differs little from an animal or plant.

His basic needs are food, drink, and sex.

Money causes these needs to expand until they cross the necessary limits. Once they begin to be pursued for their own sake as a result of wealth, the human being turns into an animal that eats and drinks.

I will not say mates, because an animal practices sex to preserve the species, whereas the human being also practices it for pleasure.

On this point, the human being is less civilised than the animal.

That, in any case, is nature’s judgment.

The ordinary person keeps his appetites under control and spends according to his means.

The rich person lets them loose.

He corrupts himself and others.

Money always carries the possibility of tyranny, as the Quran says:

Man becomes arrogant when he sees himself as self-sufficient.

Tyranny has two sources: power and money.

The first appears in Nahj al-Balagha:

Whoever gains power becomes a despot.

That is the nature of power, as Ibn Khaldun diagnosed it, and the nature of wealth, as the Quran diagnosed it.

We see an example of it today in the power of financial oligarchies over Western politics, driving aggression against other peoples to the point of threatening entire countries with nuclear destruction.

There is no remedy for this disaster except to answer the call of Eastern thinkers and redistribute wealth among the people so that it cannot accumulate in a few hands.

In other words: prevent hoarding and confiscate concentrated wealth wherever it appears.

Western bourgeois culture portrays this principle as a form of religious asceticism.

That is an act of appropriation that ignores the actual relationship between religion and luxury, and ignores the staggering cost of religion itself: its clergy, its institutions, its buildings, its ceremonies, and the comfortable lives of religious officials.

Western bourgeois culture also confuses Sufism with religion and Taoism with religion.

As we have now seen, Sufism is religion’s opposite and its greatest rival.

Taoism did not confront religion in the first place, because China and Chinese civilisation had no religion in the relevant sense.

The Eurasian struggle between religion and philosophy was unknown in China.

We need to stop randomly merging religion and spirit.

That confusion is one of the fantasies and falsifications produced by people who distort history.

Eastern thought is not Eastern theology.

The distance between the two is the distance between reason and faith.

Religion exercised enormous power and domination, but thought had its own enormous field of counter-movement.

The life of the East cannot be reduced to the prevailing political and religious authorities.

It also contains opposition: that distant current ignored by Orientalists and by their Eastern commentators because acknowledging it would destroy the myth of the religious East.

The French Enlightenment of the eighteenth century is a small chapter beside the many chapters of Islamic and Chinese enlightenment.

For every Rousseau, Voltaire, and Montesquieu, the East has figures of comparable number and force.

But Westerners understood spirituality only through religion.

When some of them rebelled against religion, they therefore fell into crude materialism rather than scientific materialism.

Eastern thinkers, by contrast, rebelled against religion by separating religion from spirituality.

The enlightenment thinkers of Islam and China could therefore be deeply spiritual at the same time as they were heretics.

Heresy did not detach itself from the spirit.

In fact, it remained rooted in it.

Eastern history contains a sharp contrast between the pleasure-seeking clergy and the spirituality of heretics.

The Eastern ascetic—at least within the traditions of Islam and China—is modest, restrained, and loving toward ordinary people.

The religious official and the official of the state are greedy, arrogant, and hostile to them.

Religiosity does not require asceticism.

The Muslim sultans who came after Ali ibn Abi Talib were religious, perhaps in many cases more overtly religious than Ali himself, apart from a small number of openly dissolute rulers such as al-Walid ibn Yazid.

At the same time, they were pleasure-seekers.

Harun al-Rashid used to pray one hundred additional units of prayer each day, even though Muhammad’s own prayer did not exceed eleven. He would make pilgrimage one year and wage jihad the next.

At the same time, Harun was a sexual brute and an animal of pleasure.

This is the general description that applies to the rulers of Islamic states, apart from a handful such as Nur al-Din the Martyr and Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi.

Salah al-Din was both devout and ascetic, perhaps because of his Kurdish formation.

But the general pattern among the great majority of sultans was religiosity combined with pleasure-seeking.

Religious authorities, meanwhile, preached asceticism and made it a requirement of popular religion—that is, the religion of ordinary people.

This is one of their tricks.

Material enjoyment is left to the elite while deprivation is imposed on everyone else.

The relationship between elites and the clergy requires no explanation.

It is one of the most persistent facts of history.

Sufism was not a perfectly coherent movement.

In fact, as a movement, its negative side was larger than its positive side.

All sorts of people entered it: good and corrupt, honest and treacherous, ascetic and opportunist.

The lesser Sufis cannot be praised as a group. We have to choose among them.

There were young people who dissolved into the Sufi sensibility, cared deeply, and sincerely loved God through the human women they loved.

Many others mixed the Sufi path with foreign additions they had brought in from outside.

The movement was subjected to a great deal of harsh criticism.

Sufis became proverbial examples of objectionable conduct.

One saying quoted by al-Zabidi in Taj al-Arus calls them, in a rhyming insult, “dancers and platter-men”—people who dance and pile food onto their plates.

There are amusing stories about the tricks some used to get food.

One Sufi supposedly had engraved on his ring:

“Its food is everlasting.”

Another had:

“Bring us our lunch.”

A Sufi from Merv was once preaching to people and made them cry.

When the crying went on too long, he took out a small lute and began to play, saying:

“After all this long grief, we need an hour of happiness.”

An amusing and delightful man.

But hardly one of the best Sufis.

Very early in the Sufi period, Shaqiq al-Balkhi said:

“I found people talking about poverty, with a new story every night. I saw the people of Damascus talking and elaborating theories, but I gained nothing from their knowledge. In Egypt I found a group I did not like. In Baghdad I saw people describing the states of the knowers, though I do not know that any of them ever reached what they talked about.”

(Ibn Asakir, 8/333)

This is what happens in a movement that gathers all kinds of people together.

They were mocked for claiming purity and for the idea that their very name came from purity.

Two satirical lines were attributed to one of their critics:

I see the Sufis as the worst of tribes— go tell them so, and spare me their pretence. Eat like the beasts if that is what you worship, and dance for me.

We examined the attribution elsewhere in our book on al-Maʿarri.

The criticism is directed at conduct contradicting the very meaning of Sufism.

Among the poems written against them are lines by Ibn Sabir al-Manjaniqi, a catapult officer from Baghdad in the first third of the seventh Islamic century.

He complains about Sufis whom he had the misfortune of receiving as guests:

My lord, O shaykh of the ribat, whose excellence and rank are plain, I come to complain of Sufi tyranny: they spent the night as guests and friends.

I brought them food and asked their leave, while all night my own belly cried with hunger. They walked all over the bread— and ascetics, after all, are famous for walking on water.

In another poem he mentions their excess in dancing and drinking and blames their shaykhs:

They put on wool and left purity behind, the shaykhs of our age, drinking their wine.

Dancing and pretty boys are their concern: long hair hanging beneath a short hem.

With Ibn Sabir the situation is neatly reversed.

Instead of a Sufi condemning the soldier, we have a soldier attacking the Sufis and accusing them of corruption.

We have to accept this as part of the movement.

It is why I prefer to speak of the Sufism of the great masters rather than of Sufism in general.

The truth of Sufism is found among its great masters, not among the mass of lesser followers.

In this respect Sufism resembles philosophy.

Philosophy developed through individual philosophers rather than through some moving current that hardened into a sect.

Sufi truth, like philosophical truth, was the work of outstanding individuals.

We should therefore avoid identifying the whole phenomenon with the movement around it.

Like philosophy, Sufism remained fundamentally an individual phenomenon whose greatness and historical influence came from its great figures, not from the miscellaneous crowds gathered beneath their name.

The same is true of Taoist philosophy.

There were minor Taoists just as there were minor Sufis, and some exploited the name of the Tao to make a living.

The greatness and historical force of Taoism lay in its exceptional figures: Laozi, Zhuangzi, Liezi, Huainanzi, and others of their rank.

Al-Sarraj al-Tusi observes in The Book of Flashes that lesser Sufis imitated the great masters before they themselves had become firmly grounded in Sufism.

He counted this among the causes of corruption and deviation among them.

The great masters differed in how directly they entered the field of social struggle.

The masters of philosophical Sufism did not immerse themselves in the daily hardships of ordinary people, although they remained committed to freedom of belief and opposed religious persecution.

They were also more flexible about relations with the state.

Like the philosophers, they built bridges toward it.

Their concerns were largely those of intellectuals: searching for the truth of things, defending freedom of thought, and protecting human life from the violence of the state.

Their own lifestyles ranged from asceticism to moderation.

None of them, however, seems to have left substantial wealth to his children.

Ibn Arabi, the one closest to rulers, left no fortune for his sons because he distributed whatever remained beyond his needs from the gifts rulers gave him.

In the field of knowledge, Ibn Arabi added enough to Islamic philosophy to place him at the head of any list of its major philosophers.

His greatest achievement was the unity of being.

Dialectical logic belongs there too.

His writings, especially the Futuhat, contain an enormous range of knowledge, some belonging to astronomy, some to the natural sciences, some to medicine, and some to other theoretical and practical fields.

He even discussed the possibility of manufacturing a human being, a scientific luxury that Jabir ibn Hayyan had dreamed of and that some modern scientists have discussed again.

It would be more useful to search for medicines capable of treating incurable diseases and extending human life.

The great masters of social Sufism also differed among themselves.

Hallaj tried the path of revolution.

He wanted to establish the state of the people on the ruins of the sultan’s state.

When they crucified him, Abu Bakr al-Shibli came to him and said:

“Did I not warn you about the world?”

The bloodshed of that experiment discouraged the others from becoming directly involved.

They turned instead toward a firm principle of boycott and opposition.

They tried to ease the condition of the people with whatever resources became available to them, while continuing to argue for making wealth common, preventing hoarding, and extending its benefits to everyone.

It was almost as though they lived waiting for someone still to come who would finally carry these principles out.

They insisted that the human tragedy lies in poverty and humiliation.

Poverty deprives a person of his right to live.

Humiliation destroys his human essence.

Poverty comes from the state.

Humiliation also arises in ordinary relationships between people, and its source is taking from others and becoming dependent on them.

Whoever takes something from another person, or asks that person to meet a need, places himself in humiliation.

The Sufis did not reject mutual exchange, provided it took place between equals.

A poor person should not take from a rich person, nor a weak person from someone powerful.

Their own distribution of gifts to poor people fell, in their view, within relations of equality.

They did not boast about what they gave or use it to establish superiority, because they themselves bore the mark of poverty.

Most of the great masters accepted openings—money sent to them by wealthy people whose character and piety they trusted. But they did not use that money for themselves. They distributed everything that came to them and lived from their own resources, such as manual work or an inheritance from their family.

When a great master had enough strength and standing, he could even wring money out of the ruler, provided it was taken by pressure rather than received as a favour. This seems to have been the way Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani operated. He was one of the strongest and most formidable of the great masters. As we saw earlier, he enjoyed intense popular support among the people of Baghdad, which put him in a position to confront the caliph. One could almost say that Baghdad in his time had two caliphs: Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani and the Abbasid caliph.

So although the Sufis forbade a poor person from taking help directly from a rich person, in order to protect his dignity, they themselves would give him money that had come into their hands and did not regard this as humiliating him.

Naturally, if the state itself had been in their hands, the problem would disappear altogether, because public money belongs to the people. This is also why they allowed the poor to take from alms-tax funds without treating the money as charity. The alms tax is an obligation and can be taken from the rich by force; voluntary charity is a gift and a favour.

Their concern with feeding the poor was matched by their concern with preserving their dignity.

They were also fairly close to one another in the degree of asceticism they practised. Obviously they ate enough to keep their bodies alive. Without that, they could not have survived. I tried otherwise myself, as I have already explained.

Their choice lay in giving up delicacies and whatever went beyond the amount needed to satisfy hunger. They could do without these things.

The same applied to clothing. They did not dress for luxury or display, but for covering and warmth. Ordinary wool and cotton were enough, and cleanliness was the condition they insisted on.

The great masters did not approve of patched robes. Those belonged to lesser Sufis who used them to attract attention. The masters dressed simply, but not in rags.

Naturally they did not live in palaces. They lived in the same kind of houses as ordinary people.

Their mount was the donkey, the animal of the poor. They reported that the Prophet rode a bare donkey without even a saddlecloth, and that riding a donkey protected a person from arrogance because aristocrats rode fine horses.

In everyday life they mixed with the poor in order to know their circumstances and give whatever help they could.

We have already seen that al-Jilani helped poor people clean lice from their clothes.

Their teaching gatherings were normally for the poor. They were uncomfortable when rich people or officials attended, and the same applied to their gatherings of music.

It was said of Sufyan al-Thawri that the poor sat in his gathering like sultans, while any rich man who attended sat at the back.

If they heard that a rich man was devout, they mocked him. The worship demanded of a rich man, in their view, was to distribute whatever wealth remained beyond his needs. Prayer and fasting would do him no good in place of that.

The great masters did not look shabby in the manner of later dervishes. As I have said, they did not wear patched clothing. Their clothes were simply inexpensive: cotton or ordinary wool.

They cleaned their teeth with the siwak, following the established practice, and among the small things they carried were a comb and a tooth-stick: the comb to keep the beard from matting and tangling, and the siwak to clean the teeth.

They also used perfume, following the practice of the son of Amina.

For them, the line between simplicity and squalor was clear. The distinction disappeared only in the later dervish age that began with the Ottomans.

A small number among them did regard bathing as a luxury, and some walked barefoot.

Bishr al-Hafi—Bishr the Barefoot—was one of these, and there is a story behind his bare feet.

He once went to a cobbler and asked him to mend a small tear in his sandal.

The cobbler said:

“How much trouble you poor Sufis cause other people!”

Bishr took off his sandals, handed them to the cobbler, and walked away barefoot. He remained barefoot after that.

Once he went to visit one of his companions and knocked at the door. A little girl came out and asked who he was.

“Bishr al-Hafi,” he said.

She went to tell her father, then asked:

“Why is he barefoot? If he bought a pair of sandals for one dirham, he would lose the name!”

Bishr was closer to severe austerity than ordinary asceticism. He lived in Baghdad at the same time as Maruf al-Karkhi, who was an ascetic without being an extreme one.

The Sufis were also accused of smoking hashish. The accusation is old; it appears in The Devil’s Delusion (p. 373).

It was probably not entirely invented. A Sufi who had not yet become firmly established on the path, had not mastered meditation, and had not developed the spiritual ability to commune with the spirit of the universe might turn to a drug in the hope of reaching the state more quickly.

A great master had no need for it. His spirit had been trained in meditation and union, and the depth of his feeling and the strength of his inward intuition made drugs unnecessary.

I would not rule out, however, that some of them drank wine for ecstasy.

Ibn al-Farid’s great wine poem strongly suggests that he drank, and Ibn al-Farid was a rapturous lover: sensitive, delicate, and intoxicated with beauty.

In truth, it is difficult to read that magnificent wine poem without wanting a drink.

Did Sufism fail?

If we accept the theory of failure so beloved by our writers, then of course it failed.

Zaki Mubarak had already announced this verdict in his foolish book on Sufism in literature. Unfortunately for him, he did not discover what Adonis later discovered through his fine critical sense and his deep literary and artistic culture.

One of Zaki Mubarak’s signs of Sufism’s failure was that his shoes were stolen whenever he entered a mosque, whereas no one stole them in modern institutions. His point was that modern culture or civilisation was therefore more successful and more useful.

His argument echoes the Orientalism that swept violently through his generation. Taha Husayn was almost the only one to escape it. Like Adonis, he combined a deep command of the heritage with serious engagement with modern culture. He was not the product of a single source or a single set of teachers. He also possessed a personal awareness and quickness of mind joined to a sound natural intelligence.

People differ in their gifts.

But Zaki Mubarak did not know how Westerners steal, or what they steal. Nor did he know how we steal, or how the theft of the poor differs from the theft of the rich.

Writers often know very little about these things because they take their ideas from books. They know little about society, its sciences, or its problems. Of the people living right beside them, they know only that they are “the common people.” Of distant peoples, they know only what they have read.

This makes it difficult for them to grasp the fine differences between civilisations, continents, and historical periods: what it means for a civilisation to rise, what it means for one to recede, and what follows from either process.

Among the people of that generation, the only one who really deserved the name thinker was Taha Husayn. The rest were critics, prose writers, narrators, and translators—with translation the profession most common among them.

Civilisations do not fall. They move from one place to another.

If we spoke of the “fall of civilisation” in the way our writers do, we would have to ask where modern civilisation itself is now.

What people call the fall of a civilisation is simply its coming to a stop in the place where it first arose and its movement somewhere else.

Several civilisations may also succeed one another in the same place, as happened in Mesopotamia.

Islamic civilisation arose during a period of civilisational interruption across the Fertile Crescent following the end of the last Babylonian age in the fifth century BCE. In Europe, this was also a period of interruption after Roman civilisation came to an end and the continent entered the darkness of its medieval centuries.

Muslims took up the Semitic inheritance together with the inheritances of the Greeks, Persians, and Indians and made from them an Islamic civilisation.

When the expansion of that civilisation slowed, its achievements had already passed into Europe.

While Muslims forgot their own scientists and philosophers, Europeans studied and developed their work. While the European intellectual proudly traced himself back to Ibn Rushd, Ibn Rushd was almost unknown in the Ottoman age.

Islamic civilisation did not fall and did not fail.

It changed its home.

After a civilisation moves elsewhere, something of it remains latent in its old home.

This survives in two storehouses.

The first is everyday life: people inherit the values of the civilisation that has moved on, preserving some of them and altering others.

The second is its written record. Texts remain in their repositories until someone discovers them and brings them back to readers, just as Muslims recovered Greek books from Roman collections.

In our own age we rediscovered the written record of Islamic civilisation. We came to know it again and fashioned from it what we now call the heritage.

Its absence from us was never as complete as the absence of Greek books had been from Muslims. Islamic culture continued through its dead period by way of commentators and transmitters. Later generations still knew the names of al-Hallaj, Ibn Sina, al-Jilani, Ibn Arabi, and others, even when they knew the names without knowing the actual history behind them.

In this sense we can speak of Sufism continuing—not as an unbroken line, but as a heritage rediscovered.

Along the way, it was misunderstood from several directions.

The Orientalists, who were the first to take a serious interest in it, treated it as part of Eastern folklore.

Modern writers such as Zaki Mubarak wrote within the Orientalist framework.

The Salafis saw it through the lens of dervish practice.

Writers on the left and liberals treated it as another form of supernaturalism.

A great deal of credit for reopening the meaning of Sufism belongs to Adonis and his modernist school. They were among the first to recognise it as a distinct current within the heritage, marked by intense poetic sensitivity and by impulses toward rebellion and freedom.

Under Adonis’s influence, a generation of writers emerged who studied Sufism, searched out its great masters, and brought it into their own writing.

We should not, however, deny the influence of Louis Massignon.

In the case of al-Hallaj, Massignon published his writings and devoted studies to him in which the valuable and the worthless, knowledge and ignorance, are all mixed together.

The present generation encountered al-Hallaj through that work, and al-Hallaj took on an image resembling that of Christ and Husayn.

But like Christ and Husayn, he was not understood through the relationship between his movement and society—as a social fighter whose movement belonged to social struggle. Instead he was presented as a victim of freedom of thought, because that was how Massignon introduced him.

This has left us with the heavy task of returning al-Hallaj to what I regard as his historical place: among the victims of social revolution, not the victims of freedom of thought.27

The rediscovery of social Sufism goes back to the martyred scholar, though for him it appeared mainly as a line of separation from the state.

The line of struggle for ordinary people—the communalist field—is our contribution.

Once rediscovered, Sufism can enter modern culture as a source of independence and rootedness instead of dependence on Western culture.

The communalist line within social Sufism can help sharpen our culture, free it from the dominance of the Western commercial law, and form intellectuals who do not merely talk about the people and the hungry but live among them and confront, beside them, the power of the state and money.

Our present culture, translated from the West, is a culture of slogans and chants shouted by an intellectual sitting on his sofa with an imported pack of cigarettes and a bottle of red wine beside him.

He may write these slogans or debate them in five-star halls, where cultural conferences are usually held.

The intellectual demands his own rights as though they were the rights of the people, and measures the patriotism of the state by how well it supports culture.

These are familiar European ideas. In Europe, culture is supported through official and semi-official institutions and universities, and intellectuals enjoy a status above that of ordinary people, greater resources, and better living conditions.

In the Eastern understanding, culture is a commitment toward people—ren.

The seriousness and sincerity of an intellectual are measured by the strength of his bond with the poor, by his willingness to surrender what the Sufis call the claims of the self, and by his ability to bring his standard of living down to that of ordinary people in keeping with the popular meaning of asceticism.

The intellectual’s personal happiness should come from serving people and struggling beside them for their rights. His pleasure comes from that achievement.

The Eastern intellectual is thin in body and strong in will.

Stoutness is suspicious. So are visible signs of comfort: expensive clothing, a luxurious vehicle grander than a donkey, or an elegant house.

No Taoist or Sufi could display such things and remain accepted within his own circle.

The presence of Sufism in our modern culture, and in the communalist struggle we expect to begin, will show that Sufism did not fail.

Nor did the communal wisdom of China fail—the wisdom from which modern Chinese communists emerged in order to root Marxism locally and put it into action through an experiment that showed that Marxism could work in the East only through the East’s own communal heritage, while in a purely Western form it remained weak and obstructive.

I saw with my own eyes what Chinese communism accomplished: it rescued a continent from servitude and a billion people from hunger.

Whatever is said about its crises, if true, comes from outside sources: Soviet or Western.

Chinese communism did not, in my view, retreat for economic reasons, as capitalist media and their followers among our own people claim. What happened was the result of a backward political system inherited from the Soviets, combined with American plotting alongside a Westernised Chinese bureaucracy.

Under the new Western dominance, the Chinese people lost many of their rights, and signs of hunger, poverty, begging, prostitution, and opium returned—things the communists had removed in order to build the clean society Zhuangzi called the Great Society.

Our intellectuals are unimpressed by Chinese communism because it is not polished, because it grants no special rights or cultural privileges, and because its peasant appearance exposes their own European taste.

They passed judgment on China’s economic development using Western statistics and accused the communists of holding it back.

But China advanced in every field under the communists and under their People’s Republic, which in its first thirty years provided food security for a billion people, who came to eat three meals a day without relying on imported food.

What should we call an economic system capable of achieving such a thing in twenty years?

After this great agricultural revolution, the communists turned toward industrialisation using their own resources.

They discovered oil after foreign experts had told them that China had none. China then achieved self-sufficiency in this strategic resource and began exporting the surplus.

The communists also achieved four major technologies: aviation, missiles, nuclear technology, and satellites.
