They made major advances in light industry as well.

Had it not been for the mutual childishness of Mao Zedong and the Soviet leaders, they might even have been able to prevent the collapse of the Soviet Union by helping solve the consumer crisis that overwhelmed it.

Glimmer

Uthman al-Marin said:

The drunkenness of ecstasy is, in its meaning, sobriety;
and the sobriety of ecstasy is drunkenness in union.

PreviousThe Orbit of Zayn al-AbidinNextThe Final Orbit

The Final Orbit

Texts and Positions

  • Ibn Asakir relates a saying attributed to Abu Hurayra (6/16):

The light of wisdom is hunger. The foundation of religion is giving up the world. Repentance before God means loving the poor and staying close to them.

This saying has no authentic basis. Nor is it one of the inventions of Abu Hurayra, who himself has been accused of fabricating hadith. It was invented by the Sufis.

  • Shaqiq al-Balkhi said:

I entered the home of Abbad ibn Kathir and found pots bubbling away, some sour and some sweet. I was surprised by what I saw. His servant said to me: “Man of Khurasan, he has not eaten meat for years. Every day he has seven pots prepared, sour and sweet, and uses them to feed the poor, the sick, and those who have no way of supporting themselves.”

Ibn Asakir, in his biography of Shaqiq (6/322).

The story suggests that Abbad ibn Kathir had money and used it to relieve other people’s suffering.

  • Shaqiq al-Balkhi once met Ibrahim ibn Adham. Ibrahim asked him:

“What first set you on the path that brought you here?”

Shaqiq replied:

I was travelling through the wilderness when I saw a bird with two broken wings stranded in a barren place. I said to myself: Let me see where its food comes from.

I sat opposite it. Before long another bird appeared with a locust in its beak and placed it in the beak of the bird with the broken wings.

I said to myself: The One who sent this healthy bird to feed a bird with broken wings in the middle of nowhere can provide for me wherever I may be.

So I stopped earning a living and devoted myself to worship.

Ibrahim said:

Shaqiq, why not be the healthy bird that feeds the injured one, and so be better than him? Have you not heard that the Prophet said, “The upper hand is better than the lower”? One sign of the believer is that in everything he does, he seeks the higher of two stations until he reaches the rank of the righteous.

Shaqiq took Ibrahim’s hand, kissed it, and said:

“You are our teacher, Abu Ishaq.”

Ibn Asakir, in his biography of Shaqiq.

Some Sufis who came out of a legal-religious background insisted on complete trust in God and on giving up work, relying on God to provide. Shaqiq’s story reflects this religious meaning of trust. Ibrahim ibn Adham, by contrast, belonged to the working Sufis. He lived from the labour of his own hands and waited for neither God nor other people to provide his livelihood. Shaqiq admitted his mistake and agreed with Ibrahim that a person should not live in dependence but should work for his food.

Junayd was asked what a person should do to earn a living. He replied: “Draw water and gather date stones.” (al-Lumaʿ, 195.) That was his answer for someone who could find no other work.

  • In al-Lumaʿ, Ibrahim ibn Shayban says:

We would not keep company with anyone who said, “My sandal.”

Because the word my implies ownership. Someone who speaks that way has stepped outside the communal relationship binding them together.

The possessive my has no place in the Sufi.

  • The People of Permissibility said that things are, by their original nature, open to everyone. Restrictions arose only because people began taking more than their share. Where there is no such encroachment, things return to their original condition of free availability.

They appealed to verses such as:

“…and We caused grain to grow in it, and grapes and fresh vegetation… as provision for you and your livestock.”

They said that this was addressed to people collectively, without assigning these things exclusively to one person rather than another. (al-Lumaʿ, 424–425.)

This corresponds to the communist organisation of human needs: things are held in common and are open to all. Each person takes enough for their needs without violating anyone else’s right and without taking more than necessary.

According to the Sufi doctrine of permissibility, things became enclosed and forbidden because people began taking them excessively: taking what they did not need, out of greed and selfishness. Remove that aggression and things return to their original state of common availability.

Some accounts confuse common ownership of wealth with women being held in common. This may simply have been an accusation added later rather than something these people themselves taught. Defenders of private property have always accused communalists of sharing women as well as wealth. The Qarmatians were accused of it, as were the Sufis, and the Mazdakites before them.

Eastern communalism means sharing wealth, not sharing women.

  • Hallaj said:

Our secrets are virgins. No deluded imagination has broken their seal.

(al-Lumaʿ, 321.)

  • In ʿAwārif al-Maʿārif:

The one who reaches the end stands on the narrow path between excess and deficiency.

The qutb—the supreme Sufi saint—orders his conduct, his private life, and his dealings with others according to the law of moderation. This includes the way he lives. His material life falls somewhere between extreme austerity and luxury, in keeping with their understanding of asceticism.

They differed among themselves. Some lived very austerely, while others were content with ordinary renunciation. Some married and others did not. Most of those who married took one wife; a smaller number had several.

The people I am concerned with here are those who lived austerely and either did not marry or married one woman.

  • Junayd was asked what the end of the path was.

He replied:

Returning to the beginning.

Some explained this by saying that a person begins in ignorance, reaches knowledge, and then returns to bewilderment and ignorance.

This concerns knowledge of God.

One of them said:

Those who know God best are the most bewildered by Him.

The reason is the problem of divinity itself, which has no philosophical or physical foundation.

But Junayd’s words can also be understood differently, through their doctrine of opposites. The more a person knows, the more ignorant he becomes. The more firmly established he becomes on the path, the more he returns to simplicity. Whoever reaches the road of truth becomes bewildered. Whoever is illuminated by the sun falls into darkness.

Nothing in existence is absolute except the First Being.

  • A saying:

A servant does not reach the reality of faith until people think he is mad.

This saying was invented by the Sufis.

Madness is one of the effects of intoxication and ecstasy: breaking free from the restraints of reason and entering the open space of the irrational.

Why Does He Not Remember God?

Al-Rudhbari:

God knows that I do not remember Him. How could I remember Him when I never forget Him?

The second half-line is awkward. Its syntax has been forced into shape to preserve the metre. I tried to repair it and could not.

What the poet means is that he does not “remember” God because he has never forgotten Him.

But there is a sleight of hand here. Normally, you remember something after having forgotten it. Yet the “remembrance of God” means praising and invoking Him; it has nothing to do with having forgotten Him in the first place.

What the poet really means is unity.

Once someone becomes one with God, becomes part of Him, and shares being with Him, how can he remember God when he himself is God?

At that point worship also loses its meaning.

He would only be worshipping himself.

  • A Sufi saying:

Nothing of the unseen appears while anything remains in the pocket.

Money blocks vision.

The rich intellectual is blind.

A story:

Shaykh Abu al-Qasim al-Iskandarani sold an animal to a man. A few days later the man came back and said:

“My master, the animal I bought from you refuses to eat anything in my house.”

The shaykh asked:

“What do you do for a living?”

The man replied:

“I dance for the governor.”

The shaykh said:

“Our animal does not eat unlawful earnings…”

The Sufis dance too.

But they dance in their own gatherings, not at the governor’s court.

  • Annihilation in humanity. Ibn Asakir relates:

Sari al-Saqati said: “I was returning from the Eid prayer when I saw a dishevelled little boy with Maʿruf al-Karkhi. I asked him, ‘Who is this?’

“He said: ’I saw the other children playing while he stood apart, miserable. I asked him why he was not playing.

“’He said: “I am an orphan. I have no walnuts.”

“‘So I thought perhaps I could go out, gather date stones, sell them, and buy him some walnuts.’”

Children still play with walnuts in our own time. Several walnuts are thrown toward a hole in the ground. If they all go in, the player takes them.

Collecting date stones also survived into our time. As children, my friends and I used to gather them and sell them to blacksmiths so that we could buy sweets and other things.

Maʿruf al-Karkhi must have reached into his pocket and found nothing he could give the boy to buy walnuts.

So he thought of going out with him, gathering date stones, selling them, and giving him the money so that he could buy his walnuts.

What would Maʿruf have done if the wealth of the state had fallen into his hands?

That is what we will do when the wealth of the state falls into ours.

Then everything will return to the people, and the worldly powers will have nothing left with which to lord it over the hungry.

The day of the oppressed against the oppressor is harder than the day of the oppressor against the oppressed.

  • The Price of Arrival. Junayd is quoted by al-Shaʿrani in al-Anwār al-Qudsiyya, in the margin of the Tabaqāt:

Among us, a man does not reach the rank of a true man until a thousand friends among the formal religious scholars testify that he is a heretic.

The “formal scholars” are the scholars of religion.

The remark suggests that the end of Sufism is the beginning of heresy.

  • What Is Sufism?

A man asked Hallaj what Sufism was while Hallaj was hanging on the cross.

He answered:

What you see is the easiest part of it.

  • Hallaj’s Communalism

A person who truly trusts in God does not eat while anyone in the town has a greater claim to that food.

(al-Anwār al-Qudsiyya.)

Here trust in God has a special meaning: leave the food to whoever needs it more, and entrust your own satisfaction to hunger.

I have a soul that will perish or rise— by your life, through me—to something great.

God’s peace and blessings be upon him, and upon us.

We are walking toward the same destination.

  • Suhrawardi the Martyr: The Shrine Is Near

I say to my neighbour, tears running down: I have resolved to leave these homes.

Let me go, and do not mourn. Of shooting stars, the noblest are those that travel.

In darkness I saw a light, as though the night had dressed itself in day.

How long must fish be my companions? How long must the dragon be my neighbour?

How long should I accept a home in the wasteland when I have built my house above the two Farqad stars?

A flash comes to me from Sanaʿa, reminding me how near the shrine has become.

  • Dreams

Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani once saw the funeral of a sinner and slipped into a hallway so that he would not have to pray over him.

Later someone saw the dead man in a dream and asked:

“What did God do with you?”

He replied:

“He forgave me.”

Then he said:

Tell Ayyub: “Say: If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord’s mercy, you would hold them back for fear of spending them.”

A fierce dream.

It rebukes the person who puts punishment before mercy and condemns everyone who differs from him to destruction.

  • A Reproach in a Dream

Abu Bakr al-Rashidi said:

I saw Muhammad al-Tusi the teacher in a dream. He told me:

“Say to Abu Saʿid al-Saffar:

We pledged never to turn away from love. Yet, by the life of love, you left us—we did not leave you.”

I woke up and told Abu Saʿid.

He said:

“I used to visit his grave every Friday. This was the one Friday I failed to go…”

  • They said—and wrongly attributed it to Sufyan al-Thawri:

Those who neglect the foundations are barred from arrival. Anyone who does not hold to necessity in what he says and does will never be able to keep food, drink, and sleep within the measure of need. Once he goes beyond necessity, the resolve of his heart begins to collapse.

In other words, natural needs must not be exceeded in the search for perfection and advancement.

The foundation is strength of resolve. A person must not do anything that weakens it.

Strength is one of the qualities of the Sufi.

  • Where Does Prayer Lead?

A man asked Shibli about what mattered in prayer.

He replied:

Cast your whole concern toward the higher world, and from there toward the lower world, until it breaks open in your heart that there is nothing but God…

Ibn Asakir, 2/245.

  • Their State at Death

Junayd was dying. Someone said:

“Say: There is no god but God.”

He replied:

I never forgot Him. Why should I remember Him now?

Abu Yaʿqub al-Nahrajuri was dying. They asked the same of him.

He replied:

By the might of the One who never tastes death, nothing stands between Him and me except the veil of His majesty.

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri was dying. They asked him for some final advice.

He said:

Do not distract me. I am astonished by the beauty of His gentleness.

Ibn Sahl al-Isfahani said:

Do you imagine that I will die the way ordinary people die, from illness or something of that kind? I will simply be called, and I will answer.

One day he was walking when he suddenly said:

At Your service.

And died.

Abu Amr al-Istakhri said:

I saw Abu Turab al-Nakhshabi in the desert, standing upright and dead, with nothing holding him up.

  • The Challenge

Ibrahim al-Khawwas said:

Nothing ever frightened me without my going straight into it.

Whatever terrified him, he confronted.

  • Sufi Ethics

Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said:

Among the most important rules we followed when we first gathered in the mosque of Abu Uthman were these:

Whatever came to us, we gave others the first claim to it.

We never went to sleep with anything guaranteed in our possession—that is, we did not sleep with money in our pockets that we had not distributed.

If someone treated us badly, we did not take revenge for ourselves. We apologised to him and humbled ourselves before him.

And whenever we felt contempt for anyone in our hearts, we got up and served him.

(al-Ghunya by al-Kilani, 2/183.)

  • Christian Echoes

In al-Qushayri:

If someone asks: What predominates in the saint when he is sober?

The answer is: truthfulness in fulfilling what he owes to God; then gentleness and compassion toward creation in every state; then a mercy broad enough to include all creation; then patient endurance of them with good character; then eagerness to ask God to show them kindness without waiting for them to ask; then concern for their salvation; refusal to retaliate against them; guarding himself against resentment toward them; keeping his hands away from their wealth; abandoning every kind of greed; restraining his tongue from speaking badly of them; refusing to dwell on their faults; and refusing to be anyone’s enemy either in this world or in the next.

(p. 160.)

  • Absolute Rights

Sufyan ibn Uyayna said:

There are four things for which you owe no account: satisfying hunger, quenching thirst, covering nakedness, and finding shelter.

Ibn Qutayba, ʿUyūn al-Akhbār, Book of Asceticism.

That means:

food, drink, clothing, and housing.

These are absolute human claims. A person has the right to obtain them by whatever means are necessary and cannot be held to account for doing so.

The principle includes stealing and forcibly taking money from those who possess it when a person needs that money to obtain these necessities.

Does it also mean that a woman may sell her body to obtain the money she needs for these four things?

Certainly not.

Sufyan’s words mean taking money from those who possess it by force if necessary. They do not permit a person to sell honour or dignity, because that contradicts the essence of being human.

Within these limits, theft and fraud do not.

The point is therefore one of resistance, not humiliation or surrender.

  • The Hunger of the Ruler

The Prophet Joseph was asked:

“Why do you go hungry when you control the treasuries of the land?”

He replied:

I am afraid that if I eat my fill, I will forget the hungry.

This story was created by the opposition to establish a principle: the ruler must live austerely and remains responsible for the hungry.

Its meaning is also contained in the Iraqi saying about the full man and the hungry man: the people go hungry because their rulers and their intellectuals are full.

  • He Dies at the Front

Ibrahim ibn Adham died in Byzantine territory, fighting the Europeans.

When he felt death approaching, he said:

String my bow for me.

He took hold of it and died with the bow in his hand.

I should add that the tomb bearing his name in Jableh, in the Latakia region, cannot really be his grave.

It can only be treated as a memorial.

  • Read Them!

Abu al-Qasim al-Nasrabadi:

Comfort is a vessel filled with reproach.

Abu Saʿid al-Kharraz:

My greatest sin toward Him is that I know Him.

Junayd:

I once fell ill and asked God to cure me. He said to me inwardly: “Do not come between Me and yourself.”

Sahl al-Tustari:

For thirty years I have been speaking to God, while people imagine I am speaking to them.

Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri:

Fire burns whoever can feel it. But if a man is himself the fire, how can he burn?

Another said:

God, You know how incapable I am of thanking You as You deserve. So thank Yourself on my behalf!

Abu Salih Muflih al-Hanbali:

The world is forbidden to the heart but lawful to the self. Everything you are permitted to look at with the eye in your head, you are forbidden to look at with the eye of your heart.

The body is the garment of the heart.

The heart is the garment of the inner heart.

The inner heart is the garment of consciousness.

Consciousness is the garment of the secret.

The secret is the garment of knowledge.

Hallaj:

I saw a bird among the birds of Sufism. It had two wings. It broke away from me just as it was about to fly.

It asked me about purity.

I said: “Cut off your wing with the shears of annihilation, or do not follow me.”

It said: “Then what wing am I to fly with?”

I said: “Poor fool! Nothing is like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.”

That day the bird stopped in the sea of understanding and drowned.

(Tā-Sīn of the Point.)

  • Ibn Ata Allah al-Iskandari

The whole universe is darkness. It is lit only by the appearance of the Real within it.

To ask Him for something is to accuse Him.

Hope is hope only when accompanied by action. Otherwise it is merely a wish.

Every word that comes out of a person wears the clothing of the heart it came from.

Whatever you love, you become its slave.

The less there is to delight you, the less there will be to grieve you.

He lets harm come to you through their hands so that you will not rest your heart in them. He wants to unsettle you from everything, so that nothing can distract you from Him.

The universe is larger than you only in bodily terms. In spiritual terms, it cannot contain you.

The human spirit is wider than the universe.

Anyone living inside the universe whose horizons toward the unseen have not opened remains imprisoned by his surroundings and confined within the structure of his own self.

  • Knowledge and Ordinary People

Malik ibn Dinar said:

When a servant learns in order to put his knowledge into practice, knowledge increases him in knowledge. When he learns for some other purpose, it only increases him in corruption and arrogance, and he begins to despise ordinary people.

He is describing the intellectual who turns the authority of culture against the people, looks down on them, and treats them with contempt because he calls them ignorant.

Ordinary people may be illiterate.

That does not make them ignorant.

An illiterate person can be alert and aware of many things that escape the intellectual.

Ignorance can coexist with education.

Knowledge can coexist with illiteracy.

  • Junayd:

When love becomes true, the rules of propriety fall away.

Perhaps this points toward freedom from formal worship at the stage of qutbhood, the highest rank of sainthood.

  • Abu Uthman al-Maghribi:

The knower is consumed in the seas of realisation.

  • Hallaj:

The mark of the knower is that he has emptied himself of both this world and the next.

  • The Sufi and the Soldier

In al-Shaʿrani’s Tabaqāt:

Shaykh Abd al-Rahman al-Dawudi was eating fish when someone told him that some soldiers had eaten on the bank of the river where his fish were caught. When they finished, they shook the remains from their tablecloth into the river, and the fish rushed to eat them.

The shaykh never ate fish again.

Some of the soldiers’ food had entered the bodies of the fish. They were no longer fit to eat…

  • From Shuʿayb Abu Madyan

Three of the most harmful companions are a heedless scholar, an ignorant Sufi, and a preacher who flatters power.

He places ignorance beside education.

An ignorant Sufi.

No one reaches pure freedom while any remnant of himself remains.

The traveller is going toward Him. The knower is going from Him.

The knower stands at a higher stage than the traveller.

The end returns to the beginning.

Discipline of the body means keeping the limbs from what harms them. Discipline of the heart means refusing to rest in the worldly powers. Discipline of the self means giving up claims about oneself.

Keeping the limbs from harm means not taking into the body what damages it.

The “worldly powers” are the state, the rich, and the religious establishment.

Giving up claims means humility: not boasting of having “arrived.”

When the knower drowns in the seas of realisation, his personality disappears. There is no longer a self there from which a boast could arise.

Spiritual chivalry means seeing what is good in people and becoming absent from their faults.

Spirits are care; bodies are protection. This is tasted, not read.

This path is founded on seriousness, effort, and breaking with what is familiar and habitual.

Sufism breaks through the familiar.

It leaves the rational behind.

It is an emigration from home.

Any truth that does not erase the servant’s traces and fixed forms is not truth.

Thought is a process of erasure and change.

Anyone whom truth does not change does not belong to it.

  • An Example

Ibn Kathir says of Shaykh Abd Allah al-Yunini:

He was known as the Lion of Syria. He came from a village near Baalbek called Yunin. He had a Sufi lodge there which people visited.

He was one of the great righteous men, famous for worship, spiritual discipline, commanding what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

His commitment to asceticism and moral scruple was extraordinary. He accumulated nothing. He owned neither money nor clothing. What he wore was borrowed. In summer he wore no more than a shirt; in winter he put a fur garment over it. On his head he wore a cap made of goatskin.

He regularly went out to fight—against the Crusaders and Byzantines—and shot with a bow whose draw weight was eighty ratls.

At times he withdrew to Mount Lebanon. In winter he went to the springs of Ayn al-Asal, on the eastern side of the mountain overlooking the village of Duma east of Damascus, because the water there was warm. People would come to visit him there.

At other times he came to Damascus and stayed at the foot of Mount Qasioun.

He was known for unusual spiritual states and visions.

People called him the Lion of Syria.

He would never stand up for any ruler. He said:

“You stand only for the Lord of the Worlds.”

When al-Amjad, the ruler of Baalbek, came to him, the ruler would sit before him. The shaykh would say:

“Amjad, you did this and this.”

He would command him and forbid him, and al-Amjad would obey everything he said.

He accepted gifts but kept nothing until the next day.

When hunger became severe, he took almond leaves, rubbed them together, swallowed them, and drank cold water afterward.

They also claimed that in some years he travelled to the pilgrimage through the air.

The day before his death, he climbed to his lodge. He spent the night remembering God and remembering his companions and everyone who had ever shown him even the smallest kindness, and he prayed for them.

When morning came, he prayed with his companions. Then he leaned back and continued remembering God, holding his prayer beads.

He died sitting like that.

He did not fall.

The beads did not fall from his hand.

Al-Amjad came and saw him in that condition. He said:

“Why not build a structure around him like this, so that people can continue to see the miracle?”

They told him:

“That is not the Prophetic practice.”

So the body was moved and buried beneath the almond tree under which he used to sit remembering God.

He had lived beyond the age of eighty.

He died in 617 AH.

Abu Yazid al-Bistami

I am amazed that anyone who knows God can still worship Him.

This resembles another saying:

Whoever knows the Real does not worship the Real.

I kept watch over the heart for forty years. Then I looked into myself and saw that it was the Lord, and the Lord was the servant.

God, You created these people without their knowledge and placed Your trust upon them without their consent. If You do not help them, who will?

The wish of the knower in this world is that faith survive. His wish in the next is that creation be forgiven.

As long as a servant believes there is someone in creation worse than himself, he is arrogant.

A person should never imagine that he has some superiority over other people or that he is better than they are.

He should look instead at himself and say:

“I am worse than the others.”

  • Someone asked him:

“Can anything veil the knower from his Lord?”

He replied:

If he himself is the veil, what else could possibly veil him?

The Real looked into the inner secrets of the whole world and saw them empty of Him, except for my secret. He found it filled with Him. Then He addressed me in honour and said:

“All the world are My servants except you…”

  • He once set out for the pilgrimage.

Somewhere along the road, a man met him and asked:

“Where are you going?”

“To the pilgrimage.”

“How much money do you have?”

“Two hundred dirhams.”

The man said:

Walk around me seven times and give me the two hundred dirhams. I have a family to support.

So Abu Yazid walked around him seven times and gave him the two hundred dirhams.

  • A man asked him:

“How are you this morning?”

He replied:

There is no morning and no evening. Morning and evening belong only to someone who is confined by attributes. I have no attribute.

One night I went looking for my heart and could not find it.

Near dawn I heard a voice say:

“Abu Yazid, here you are looking for something other than Us?”

The most complete quality of the knower is that the qualities of the Real flow through him, and a kind of lordship flows from him.

He was asked:

“What is Sufism?”

He replied:

A quality of the Real that the servant puts on like a garment.

There are two paradises: the paradise of bliss and the paradise of knowledge. The paradise of knowledge is eternal. The paradise of bliss is temporary.

A man asked:

“How do I reach Him?”

He replied:

Disappear from the road and you will reach Him.

A man came and knocked on his door.

Abu Yazid asked:

“Who are you looking for?”

“Abu Yazid.”

Abu Yazid replied:

So am I. I have been looking for Abu Yazid for twenty years.

When a person finds himself, he is given a choice. When he loses himself, he becomes the chooser.

The first is passive.

The second is active.

And activity is closer to dignity than passivity.

I wish the Day of Resurrection would come so that I could pitch my tent at the gate of Hell.

Someone asked:

“Why, Abu Yazid?”

He replied:

Because I know that when Hell sees me it will go out, and I will become a mercy to creation.

I crossed the barren places until I reached the wilderness. I crossed the wilderness until I reached the heavenly kingdom. I crossed the heavenly kingdom until I reached the King.

I said: “With permission?”

He said: “I have given you everything you have seen.”

I said: “You know that I saw none of it.”

He said: “Then what do you want?”

I said: “I want not to want.”

He said: “Granted.”

When I reached His Oneness, and the first glimpse of unity came to me, I travelled through Him with understanding for ten years.

Then my understanding itself became a bird whose body was made of Oneness and whose wing was made of eternity.

I flew through the air of how-ness for another ten years. I flew a distance eight hundred million times greater than the distance between the Throne and the earth.

I continued until I passed beyond permanence itself.

Then I looked out over unity, where creation disappears from the knower and the knower disappears from creation.

I vanished into the world of divine power, crossed the seas of the heavenly kingdom, and passed through the veils of divinity until I reached the Throne.

I found it empty.

So I threw myself upon it.

Moses wanted to see God.

I never wanted to see God.

He wanted to see me.

In this world He tricks you with the marketplace, and in the next world He tricks you with the marketplace.

You are forever a slave of the marketplace.

What is Hellfire?

By God, if I saw it, I would put it out with the edge of this patched cloak.

My heart is one.

My concern is one.

My spirit is one.

He heard a man say:

“All creation stands beneath the banner of our master Muhammad.”

Abu Yazid said:

By God, my banner is greater than Muhammad’s banner. My banner is made of light. Beneath it stand all humans and jinn, together with the prophets.

Glory be to me! Glory be to me! How great is my majesty!

Nothing like me exists in heaven, and no quality like mine is known on earth.

I am He, and He is I, and He is He.

  • One day Abu Yazid washed his shirt outdoors. A companion said:

“Hang it on the vineyard wall.”

He replied:

“Its owner has not given me permission.”

“Then hang it on the tree.”

“The branches might break and be damaged.”

“Then spread it on the ground.”

“The grass would dry beneath it.”

So Abu Yazid turned his back to the sun, laid the shirt across his own back and head, waited until it dried, and put it on again.

  • A Zoroastrian was told in Abu Yazid’s time:

“Become a Muslim.”

He replied:

If Islam is what Abu Yazid practises, I could never bear it.

And if Islam is what you practise, I have no desire for it.

Women and Sufism

The Sufis allowed a woman to receive the Sufi cloak of initiation from an unrelated man.

If her husband tried to prevent her, she could seek separation from him and go to her shaykh.

Sufism and Heresy

Ibn Aqil, one of the Hanbali theologians, said that much Sufi language points toward doing away with religious mediation and even prophecy itself.

When the Sufis spoke of hadith scholars, he said, they mocked them for having “taken their knowledge from one dead man after another.”

In this way, Ibn Aqil argued, they had already undermined prophecy.

And anyone who says:

My heart told me directly from my Lord

has openly declared that he has no need of the Messenger.

Ibn Aqil also said:

The heretics never dared openly reject religious law until the Sufis came along.

(Talbīs Iblīs, 372–374.)

From the Words of the Sultan of Lovers

I pray, and sing of her. When I recite, it is her remembrance that fills me.

I sway with joy inside the prayer niche while she stands there before me.

On pilgrimage, when I enter consecration for the House, I enter in her name.

To abstain from her would be the breaking of my fast.

Whom could I follow in love if I ever sought escape from it?

Every imam in love follows me.

In every limb there is a longing for her, a yearning that pulls me by the reins.

Increase my bewilderment through the excess of love for You,

and let Your burning heat run through the veins of the earth.28

And when I ask to see You as You truly are, then appear—

and do not answer me: “You shall not see.”29

O heart, you promised me patience in loving them.

Take care, then, not to grow cramped or weary.

Tell those who came before me, and those who will come after,

and everyone who looks upon my grief:

take from me, follow my example,

listen to me, and speak of my affliction among the people.

I was alone with the Beloved. Between us was a secret

finer than the breeze when it begins to move.

I stood bewildered between His beauty and His majesty,

until the language of the state itself began to speak for me.

Be coy—you are made for it. Rule me: beauty has given you the right.

The command is yours. Judge my soul however you wish,

for beauty itself has appointed you over me.

Test me in your love however you please.

My only choice is whatever pleases you.

In every state you have a greater claim on me than I have on myself,

for without you I would never have been.

Beauty veiled in majesty leaves the lover lost,

until even torment becomes sweet.

Leave me my eyes. Perhaps one day before I die

I may see with them someone who has seen you.

How far I am from what I sought!

And how could my eye receive its share when it has never seen you?

Everyone touched by beauty loves you, but I alone love everyone within your sanctuary.

The lovers will be gathered beneath my banner,

and every beautiful one beneath yours.

Your distance from me is itself a kind of nearness,

and inside your coldness I have found tenderness.

Whenever you disappear outwardly from my sight,

I turn inward in a thousand directions and find you a thousand times.

It is no wonder that light is borrowed from my outward form,

when my inward being is your home.

From the Great Ode Rhyming in Tāʾ

The Jewel of Cosmic Beauty

Speak of beauty as absolute. Do not confine it

by tying it to ornament and decoration.

The beauty of every beautiful man is borrowed from hers,

and so is the beauty of every beautiful woman.

Through her, Qays fell mad for Lubna. Through her, every lover has fallen—

Majnun for Layla, Kuthayyir for Azza.

Every one of them longed for an attribute she had put on,

a beauty appearing inside a beautiful form.

It was only she appearing through different manifestations.

They imagined someone else, although it was she who appeared within them.

She appeared by hiding and hid by appearing,

taking on one form after another in every manifestation.

At the beginning of creation she appeared to Adam

in the form of Eve, before Eve became a mother.

He fell in love with her so that through her he might become a father,

and through the pair the law of children might appear.

She has never stopped appearing and disappearing,

according to the needs of every time and every age.

She appears to lovers in every form,

clothed in astonishing shapes of beauty.

At one time she is Lubna. At another, Buthayna.

For a while she is called Azza.

They are not other than her, yet neither are they simply her.

No one shares her beauty with her.

So it is through union with her beauty

that she appeared to me adorned within others.

And I appeared for her inside every passionate lover,

whatever beautiful face and whatever name he bore.

They are not other than me in love.

I came before them, in the ancient nights.

These people are nothing but me in their love for her.

I merely appeared to them clothed in every form:

now as Qays, now as Kuthayyir,

now as Jamil, the lover of Buthayna.

Under all those names it was really I who was named.

I was the one appearing to myself through selves that disappeared.

I have never ceased to be her, and she has never ceased to be me.

There is no difference:

my own being loved itself.

The Strength of the Sufi

My soul went on feeding itself with longing, erasing power through weakness

until weakness itself became strength.

There I found all beings united in declaring

that they were branches of a trunk that was mine.

With one thought I swept across the horizons,

and with one step I pierced the seven heavens.

The bodies of those in whom no remnant of self remained

became light as spirits in my gathering.

Whoever spoke, whoever rose,

whoever displayed power, did so through a subtle thread of strength from me.

No one ever walked on water, flew through the air,

or entered fire except through my spiritual force.

Whoever received from me even one subtle thread

could act upon his whole gathering in a moment.

If the slightest subtle force from me were to enter a dead man,

his soul would return and he would live again.

Such is the soul:

when it casts away its desires, its powers multiply,

until every atom yields its strength to it.

All Religions Equal in Truth

If revelation lights the prayer niche of a mosque,

the Gospel likewise blesses the sanctuary of a church.30

And there are the books of Moses’ Torah,31

with which the rabbis commune every night.

And if a devotee bows before stones inside the Buddhist temple,32

there is no ground for sectarian condemnation.

Through me the warning reached everyone who sought it,

and through me every community has its excuse.

The eyes of no religion have gone astray,

nor the thoughts of any sect.

The Magians worshipped fire, and for a thousand ages it did not go out,

as the old accounts tell us.

Yet they intended none but me—

even when they thought they intended someone else,

and even when they themselves did not know the intention in their hearts.

Ibn al-Farid is saying what all the great Sufi poles say:

Muslims, Christians, Jews, Magians, Buddhists, and pagans are all in the right!

The Interpreter of Desires

Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi dedicated this poem to a young woman named Nizam. He speaks of his longing for her in a way that shows both Sufi abstraction and poetic embodiment, and from there moves into his doctrine of the unity of religions, his rejection of religious conflict, and his view of the pilgrimage.

I have rearranged the poem—cutting some lines and moving others—so that it comes closer to the Sufi sensibility:

O doves among the trees and branches, be gentle.

Do not double my sorrow with your grief.

Be gentle. Do not reveal through mourning and tears

the hidden force of my passion, the grief buried inside me.

Who will give me back the gathering at al-Muhassab in Mina?

Who will give me Dhat al-Athl? Who will give me Nuʿman?

Hour after hour she circles my heart,

in longing and torment, kissing all its corners,

just as the best of messengers circled the Kaaba—

though the proof of reason itself would call that House deficient.

He kissed its stones though he could speak,

and what is the rank of a house beside the worth of a human being?

The spirits lamented in the grove of gazelles.

The branches bent over me until I too was undone.

I lay fallen between breastbone and heart.

What a wonder: a garden in the middle of fire.

Before today I used to reject my companion

if his religion was not close to mine.

But now my heart has become open to every form:

a pasture for gazelles, a monastery for monks,

a temple of fire, a Kaaba for the pilgrim,

tablets of Torah and the pages of the Quran.

I follow the religion of Love.

Wherever Love’s caravan turns, that is my religion

and that is my faith.

This is one of the most important poetic texts in the whole tradition.

We read it for what it says, not for its poetry as such. As I noted earlier, Ibn Arabi’s poetic gift is not as spontaneous or overflowing as that of his contemporary Ibn al-Farid. Ibn al-Farid was a true professional poet.

Ibn Arabi writes poetry the way scholars do.

Sufi Figures

In Shadharāt al-Dhahab, under the events of 386 AH, we read of Abu Talib al-Makki:

He came from the mountain region and settled in Mecca, which is why he became known as al-Makki.

He practised severe spiritual discipline. It was even said that for a time he gave up ordinary food altogether and lived on wild plants that were lawful to eat, until his skin turned green.

He came to Baghdad and preached to the people, but began saying strange and confused things, and they abandoned him.

Muhammad ibn Tahir al-Maqdisi says in his book on genealogies that when Abu Talib al-Makki entered Baghdad, people gathered around him. He began mixing things together in his speech, and one statement in particular was remembered:

“Nothing is more harmful to the creature than the Creator.”

After this, people abandoned him and he stopped preaching.

Abu Talib al-Makki is normally classified as a Sunni Sufi.

But Sufis resemble one another in their ecstatic excesses because they all return to the same source.

Even a Sunni, believing Sufi remains closer to a deist Sufi—or even an atheist Sufi—than he is to the jurist.

Abu Madyan Frightens the Sultan

According to al-Istiqsāʾ, Abu Madyan Shuʿayb ibn al-Husayn settled in Bejaia toward the end of his life.

Large numbers of people gathered around him, and miracles were attributed to him.

Some of the formal religious scholars denounced him to Yaʿqub al-Mansur.

They told the ruler:

We fear for your state because of this man. He resembles the Mahdi, and he has followers in every country.

Yaʿqub wrote to the governor of Bejaia ordering him to send Abu Madyan to him. He instructed the governor to treat him with care and not transport him like an ordinary prisoner.

Abu Madyan died on the journey near Tlemcen in 594 AH.

The Madness of the Sufi

Ibn Sabʿin:

Do not be afraid of your madness at this stage.

It is a more complete world.

On the Search for Truth

Ibn Sabʿin:

I seek refuge in God from an aspiration that stops.

Indeed, I seek refuge in God from a mind that is ever satisfied.

The Essence of the Human Being

Ibn Arabi:

O white pearl, ruby-bright,

mounted in a shell of human flesh.

The people of the earth, miserable in their ignorance,

failed to know its worth while fighting over pearls and rubies.

Beyond Books

Ahmad ibn Abi al-Hawari threw his books into the sea and said to them:

You were excellent guides.

But once a person has arrived, remaining occupied with the guide is impossible.

Hallaj said:

Whoever points toward Him is merely a would-be Sufi.

Whoever points from Him is a Sufi.

And:

My frame is body, my inmost core is light.

My spirit belongs to the Eternal, the knowing Judge.

Through spirit it rises to the lords of spirit,

while the bodily frame remains behind as dust and decay.

The Path at the End

Al-Qushayri relates that Abraham once received a Zoroastrian as a guest.

Abraham told him:

“If you become a Muslim, I will feed you.”

The Zoroastrian replied:

“What favour would you then have done me?”

And he left.

God then revealed to Abraham:

Abraham, would you feed him only if he changed his religion?

We have been feeding him for seventy years while he remained an unbeliever…

(p. 63.)

See what we wrote earlier in the Orbits about the Sufi’s universalism and his equality between religions.

Reports of the Communalists

Al-Jahiz relates in The Book of Animals, on the authority of al-Asmaʿi:

An elderly man from Medina told me:

“This land originally belonged to people who first developed it and dug its channels.

“When the fruit ripened, one of them would say:

“‘Open the garden so that passers-by may eat from it, and so that anyone in need can take some.’

“Then he would say:

“‘Send so much to this person, and so much to that person.’

“And after the fruit had been sent, he might say:

“‘Send this many dinars to so-and-so, and that many to someone else.’

“At that point the steward would cry out:

“‘What are you doing, man? Damn you!’

“Then the land was fully developed and became rich.

“It was granted to a different set of people.

“Now every one of them walls off his garden and hides its gate.”

The story points to a struggle between two tendencies: the communal tendency and the feudal one.

The right of ordinary passers-by to take fruit from a garden was recognised in religious law, and the owner was not permitted to prevent it.

One Syrian form of this was the Garden of the Jar, which survived until the beginning of this century. It disappeared only with the arrival of the capitalist economy under the French.

A large jar—something like an enormous storage pot—would be placed at the entrance to the garden and filled with its fruit. When the garden gate was shut, passers-by could take what they needed from the jar.

Unfortunately, Iraq never developed this kind of garden because of the destruction of social values inflicted on it during the Ottoman period.

We will restore the principle in a more complete form:

by making the whole state communal.

The Kaaba of Najran

Before Islam, the Christians of Najran maintained an institution that provided free food and lodging both to the people of Najran and to travellers who came there.

Al-Aʿsha mentioned it in one of his poems:

I visit Yazid and Abd al-Masih, and Qays—the finest of its lords—

and the Kaaba of Najran, which calls you onward

until at last you reach its gates.

The Arab Christians remained closer to the memory of Christ.

The European Church had not yet come between them and him.

Address, Glad Tidings, and the Announcement of the Time

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Niffari

He made me stand before Him and said:

Tell the night: Do not become morning. You will not return after this. I will bring up the sun from where it vanished beyond the earth and hold it back from moving. It will burn whatever once sheltered in your shade and make plants grow without water. I will reveal them from every side. I will let the beasts graze on your growth, while My own growth rises tall and beautiful. Its eyes will open and they will see Me. I will make My case, and they will write down My proof through their faith.

The towering mountain will split from its base, though the waters had once stood upon its summit and it would not drink. I will lower the bed of the water. I will stretch out the noonday heat and not let afternoon follow it.

There they will gather, and I will overturn every vessel.

You will see the bird roaming freely in its own nest. You will see the one at rest purchase wakefulness with sleep, and ransom war with peace.

And He said to me:

Tell the one spread wide and stretched out:

Prepare yourself for your rule. Adorn yourself for your station. Veil your face with something translucent. Keep company with the one who shelters you with his own face, for you are My face rising from every face.

Take faith as the pledge of your covenant.

When you go out, enter into Me, until I kiss you between the eyes and whisper to you what no one but you should know. I will go out with you onto the road, and your companions will be adorned as though they were hearts without bodies.

When you are firmly upon the road, stop there, for that is your destination.

Thus says the Lord:

Stretch out your right hand and raise your banner with it.

Do not sleep and do not wake until I come to you.

Servant, stand for Me. You are My bridge and the stairway of My remembrance. Across you I pass to My companions.

I have set you in place and cast over you a shoulder of wind. I want to bring forth My knowledge that has never yet gone forth, array it as an army, and send them across you. They will follow what lies beyond you without a road.

I will reveal it, and you will not know where it came from: whether it stood before them or arose along their path.

When you see Me, move, and they will move with you. I will set you upon My hand.

Let everything pass behind you.

Whoever crosses over you, receive him and carry him.

Whoever goes around you is utterly lost.

Servant, stand within the Law, for I have made you stand there.

Leap to avenge your longing as a starving lion leaps upon its prey.

Rise and reach through Me. Seek Me through My sustaining power in everything you attain.

Whoever sees Me sees what neither appears nor hides.

Servant, your time has come.

Gather My people around you. Store My treasures with the keys I have given you.

Hold firm, and firmer still. You have reached the threshold of your full strength.

Appear before Me in what I have made you appear in.

Speak of Me through My merciful grace, so that whoever hears you remember Me will love Me.

Thus says the Lord:

I am rising over the horizon, smiling.

They will gather around Me. The weak will ask Me for help. All of them will put their trust in Me.

I will send out My light, walking among them. They will greet it, and it will greet them.

Wake, sleeping one, and rise.

And you who are already standing, move toward what lies before you.

Cast your stars against the houses. Make the Pole grow beneath your finger.

Put on the ascetic robe of the Truth, and hold nothing back.

Rule belongs to you, and the staff of blessing is in your right hand.

This is what I want, and I am witness to it.

These are the lights of God. Who can take light from His light except by His permission?

This is the Truth.

Conjecture cannot grasp you through Us, and none disputes it except the ignorant.

Thus says the Lord:

Come forward. Do not turn back.

I will string the necklace for you.

Go out to the earth by My hand, and they will see Me with you and ahead of you.

Come out from behind your curtain, for I am bringing the sun up over you.

Take your destiny in your right hand.

Find your way as the winds do.

Arm yourself with the mercy that came before all things.

Do not sleep. I have lengthened your dawn, and morning has drawn close.

This is one of the signs of your Lord.

It concerns the descent of Jesus son of Mary from heaven to earth. A near time will announce it: a sign for those who have been given knowledge, and a guidance by which God guides people toward Him.

You will rescue many who do not know.

Thus says the Lord:

I have told you this so that right conduct may appear.

Lift the veils from your face.

Mount the creature that wanders the earth. Raise up My buried foundations. Carry them to Me in your own hands.

Whoever stands with you is on the right.

Whoever opposes you is on the left.

Wake, sorrowful one.

Come forth, hidden one.

Gather up your clothes and throw your wrap across your shoulder.

I will carry you across every mountain pass.

Spread yourself wide as the full moon and the sea.

Rise like the high sky.

I will send fire ahead of you. It will spare nothing and settle nowhere.

In this is a sign: the Word of God will appear, and God will reveal His friend upon the earth. He will take the friends of God as his allies, and the believers will pledge allegiance to him in Mecca.

Those are the beloved of God.

God will support them, and they will support Him.

His companions will be the entrusted guardians, equal in number to those who witnessed Badr.

They will act and be true:

three hundred and thirteen.

They are the ones who will prevail.

Thus the Lord made me stand before Him and said:

Tell the sun:

Sun, written into the order of the Lord, uncover your face. Unfold yourself from your folds.

Travel wherever your joy triumphs over your sorrow.

Send the moon ahead of you. Let the fixed stars gather around you.

Travel beneath the clouds. Rise over the depths of the waters.

Do not set in the west and do not rise in the east.

Stand still for the shade.

You are nothing but the Lord’s mercy, a portion He sends to whomever He wills.

This is God’s guidance. He guides by it whomever He wills.

This is how God sends down revelation.

Turn, you who have remained where you are.

Be at peace, hidden one.

I have let go the reins, and the Lord has sent His secret counsel ahead of you.

Thus says the Lord:

Rise, shining sun. I have stripped away the night.

Spread yourself over everything.

The crops will grow, and every tree will give its fruit by permission of its Lord.

The orphan will come out to you and grow tall.

The callers will gather around you.

You will see how My light blossoms.

Take your people with you, you who are setting out.

Prepare for the journey.

You are the light of the Lord.

The Lord has said:

You are to establish just rule among the people.

The hearts of the believers will lean toward you.

Through you the weak will grow strong and defend themselves against what they fear.

Sleeping one, come and wake.

Receive the good news.

I have sent down the table, and springs of food and drink have burst from it.

They will come to you and stand to your right and left. They will become your helpers, and they will prevail, because whoever fights them fights Me.

And I am the hearts.

Make room, you who have been confined. I have released you from captivity and opened the doors before you.

Adorn yourself, and adorn the peoples with My splendour.

I have taken sorrow away from you and filled your heart with joy.

They will line up in a single row for My coming, and I will come with clear proof.

Do not be stunned. Do not lose your way.

After this I will disappear only once.

Then I will appear and never disappear again.

You will see My ancient friends rise and rejoice.

And He said to me:

My time has come. The appointed hour of My appearance is near.

I will reveal Myself.

The weak will gather around Me and grow strong through My strength.

I will feed them and give them drink, and you will see their gratitude to Me.

Rise, sleeper.

Sleep, you who stand.

I have made calamity the captive of consolation.

I have sent down My guidance, My light, My pillar, and My signs.

Then He said to me:

Set up the couches for Me.

Spread the earth before Me with habitation and flourishing life.

Raise the hanging curtains for My arrival.

I am coming out, and My companions are with Me.

I will raise My voice. The callers will come and ask Me to shepherd them, and I will protect them.

Blessing will descend.

The tree of abundance will grow upon the earth.

Rule will belong to Me alone.

That is the measure.

That is what I desire.

From Kurdish Sufism

The Kurds are an ancient people who have inhabited the mountain region since very early times. In a later period the region became known by their name, Kurdistan. Muslim geographers had called it either the Mountain Region or the Land of the Kurds, the latter being precisely what Kurdistan means.

The Kurds never established a unified state across their whole region because of its mountainous geography. The terrain makes it extremely difficult to create a central government able to extend its authority across areas separated by severe natural barriers.

This did not, however, prevent the Kurds from remaining a single people, preserving shared characteristics, qualities, and values.

The Kurdish language survived in this politically divided environment and remained one language despite its different dialects. In this respect it resembles Arabic and Chinese, both historically and today. Some dialects became so distant from one another that mutual understanding grew difficult without a common standard language, like Standard Arabic or Putonghua in China.

The Kurds have not yet developed a single standard language that can serve everyone and become a common language of culture in the way Standard Arabic and Putonghua have done.

Because of their tribal and mountain-based social order, the Kurds did not absorb the cultural currents of the Islamic age deeply enough to produce a learned culture of their own on the same scale as the Persians and Turks.

Kurdish literature therefore remained oral until the eleventh Islamic century, the seventeenth century CE, when Ahmad Khani launched what may be called the first cultural revolution in Kurdish history.

He wrote down the old Kurdish epic Mem and Zin in Kurdish. Until his time it had been transmitted orally. He then reshaped it through his own poetic imagination and Sufi culture, so that the work bears the personal creative mark of a major writer.

Khani opened the epic with an impassioned discussion of the Kurdish question, perhaps the first of its kind in Kurdish history.

He asked:

Who made the Kurds a people deprived, ruled, and enslaved as a whole?

He spoke of their virtues: their courage, honour, noble character, and love of what is good. He argued that they did not deserve the deprivation, division, and foreign occupation under which they lived.

He called on the Kurds to revolt, on condition that they joined the sword to virtue.

The world, he said, is like a bride. You win her only through the power of the drawn sword—when, that is, a stronger rival is competing with you for her and trying to seize her from you.

The first instrument of revolution was Kurdish unity.

The Kurds were known for the instability of relations among their tribal groups, a weakness that continues to shape the course of Kurdish revolution and helps prevent it from reaching its goal.

Arab historians noticed this as well. Al-Qifti said that the Kurds were a great nation and that, were it not for their internal feuding and fighting, they would have prevailed across the lands.

Khani called for the Kurds to unite under a central leadership, liberate their country, and build their state.

Khani also said that he wrote the epic partly to rouse the Kurds and partly to answer people who claimed that Kurds knew nothing of passionate love—that among them there was neither a heart capable of love nor a beautiful woman worth loving.

Passionate love is one of the great orbits of Sufism, as we have seen throughout this book. It is one of the famous mysteries of the Sufi path.

Khani’s purpose, however, went well beyond proving that Kurdish hearts were tender and Kurdish women beautiful. He wanted to establish a written Kurdish culture capable of standing alongside Persian and Arabic culture.

He succeeded in both his project and his revolution.

Over the last two centuries Kurdish literature and writing have poured forth in a great stream. A Kurdish lexicon and Kurdish technical vocabulary have taken shape. Kurds have become able to deal with every field of knowledge in their own language, after long depending on Arabic and Persian for culture and literature.

Khani wrote in the Arabic script and adapted it successfully to Kurdish.

The move by some Kurds today toward the Latin alphabet does not, in my view, arise from any defect in the Arabic script. It belongs instead to the current fashion for imitating everything European.

It would have been better for the Kurds to return to their old script, develop it, and continue writing in it.

Ancient peoples do not lightly abandon their writing systems. The Japanese, Chinese, and Koreans continue to write in their own systems; Tibetans in Tibetan script; Mongols in Mongolian; Armenians in Armenian; and Arabs in Arabic.

And so on.

Sufism spread through Kurdistan as part of the Islamic culture written in Arabic. Some of its great masters established their lodges in the Kurdish mountains.

The best known was Adi ibn Musafir, who lived among the Īzīdīs, an old esoteric community whose name was altered in a later period into Yazīdīs.

Adi had an influence on their veneration of Satan, whose standing had already been rehabilitated by certain Sufis.

Sufi orders appeared in Kurdistan during the Ottoman age of dervishism, which followed the end of the great age of the Sufi masters.

Some of these orders nevertheless adopted Kurdish national demands.

Even in the age of dervishism, Sufism retained positive elements capable of inspiring action toward just ends. The Bektashi order played such a role in Albania, and the Sanusi order in Libya.

In Kurdistan this burden was taken up by the Naqshbandi order, which led the Kurdish revolution from the 1930s through the 1970s through the Naqshbandi master Mulla Mustafa Barzani.

After Mulla Mustafa, the Kurdish revolution in southern Kurdistan—Iraqi Kurdistan—grew weaker when leadership passed to the party he had founded to give the revolution an organisational structure.

This was a new and imported kind of party that did not express Kurdish traditions. Its leaders were educated in the West, loyal to the global capitalist system, and did not possess the hearts of the Sufis: their firmness and courage, humanised by love and by a transparent sense of humanity.

Ahmad Khani was a Sufi master of the dervish age.

He knew the different schools of Sufism thoroughly and absorbed them deeply. When he wrote his epic, he seemed almost to be taking up a broken line that had ended with Abd al-Karim al-Jili in the ninth Islamic century.

Much of his Sufism, however, was indebted to the Persian Sufis who came after al-Jili.

Among them a rapturous Sufism of love had become dominant, well suited to the Persian passion for human beauty and the beauty of nature.

They were, for the most part, lovers. They wrote about divine love through human love, continuing the ecstatic tradition of Ibn al-Farid within the Persian landscape, whose beauty seems itself to speak in art.

Ahmad Khani appears more the student of Farid al-Din Attar and Hafez of Shiraz than of the philosopher Ibn Arabi.

Literature and an overflowing sensitivity to beauty dominate his work, just as beauty fills the Kurdish landscape: a landscape combining beauty with majesty—green plains, deep and imposing valleys, towering forest-covered mountains, and springs pouring clear running water.

The epic is full of Kurdish beauty expressed through art: song, music, and dance.

It presents scenes of extravagant celebration, overflowing with art, beauty, and excessive luxury, which can remind us of the Chinese epic Dream of the Red Chamber.

There may even be a kind of conversation between the landscape of some parts of China and that of Kurdistan: the interweaving of plain and mountain, greenery and height, deep valleys and flowing springs.

Khani’s ecstatic aesthetics remain completely at home in a Sufi atmosphere.

He is faithful to his teachers and to his school, which for him becomes a way of sensing, remembering, and forming the spirit, all of it saturated with love.

He wrote the epic to prove that the Kurds were a nation of lovers, like the people for whom Abu Firas al-Hamdani spoke:

We are a people whom dark eyes melt, though we ourselves can melt iron.

The epic contains the vocabulary of Sufi doctrine at the level of the great masters.

Ahmad Khani defended Iblis. He justified Iblis’s refusal to bow before Adam on the ground that God had been premature in proclaiming Adam’s rank before Adam had displayed any great deed that would justify such elevation.

Iblis, for his part, refuses to bow to anyone but God—that is, he refuses to bow to a human being.

Yet in another chapter of the epic, Khani asks God to leave Iblis in the Fire forever so that humanity may be redeemed through him: let Iblis enter the Fire alone and no human being enter it.

Khani begins from the love of creation and compassion for people on which Sufism was founded.

He sees no distinction among human beings on account of their beliefs:

All creation, from first to last, believer and unbeliever alike, has become a manifestation of Your greatness and Your lordship.

Like the Sufis before him, he says that the whole of existence has been placed at the service of humanity, and that the human being is the centre and purpose of the world.

He also embraced the unity of being, addressing the Truth:

You cannot occupy a place, yet You dwell within Your creatures.

This is divine indwelling in existing things, as Zhuangzi also said.

Khani’s use of the word dwelling here is new within the Sufi literature of the unity of being.

God also appears as light in beautiful faces and as fire in the hearts of lovers.

It is God’s beauty that adorns the faces of beloved women and draws lovers toward them, because His heavenly attraction is embodied in them.

It was God who afflicted Khosrow with the love of Shirin, Qays with the love of Layla, and Mem with the love of Zin.

Khani classified young male lovers as mirrors of the beauty of the Divine Essence, and beloved women as manifestations of the lights of the Divine Attributes.

On this basis he rejected same-sex love, because in his scheme love is a relation between Essence and Attributes, not between Essence and Essence or between Attributes and Attributes.

He also made spirituality a condition of true love.

This is what separates the lover from the mere pleasure-seeker.

Some people who claim to love are looking for an advantage. They are not lovers.

Others seek union with the beloved. These are lovers of the body.

Still others choose suffering: a spiritual torment that becomes their true bliss.

That is Sufi love.

Those who possess it are the gnostics.

On the basis of this classification, Khani made the love of Mem and Zin a love belonging to the next world rather than this one.

Here the epic introduces an element of theological compensation, and Ahmad Khani falls into it because, despite his Sufism, he maintained his connection to religion.

After describing the hardships inflicted upon Mem and Zin by the ruler who separated them and imprisoned Mem, Khani opens a new chapter for them in the afterlife.

There they marry and live together in the bliss of paradise.

He even makes the plots of the villain Bakr serve the purpose of delivering them into the next world, after love has raised them upward and carried them to heaven.

In the course of this, Khani gives a religious interpretation of Bakr’s killing at the hands of Tajdin, Mem’s friend, comparing it to the killing of the boy in the story of Moses and al-Khidr.

But the Sufis do not place the two cases on the same level.

Bakr is a villain and conspirator, an agent of the state.

The boy in the story of al-Khidr is innocent. Al-Khidr kills him so that he will not become a cause of corruption for his parents.

The killing of the boy cannot be justified by any law except a religious law that measures the value of human life according to righteousness and belief.

Khani moved a long way from the social line of Sufism when he spoke without discomfort of the beautiful princess Zin, served by a hundred attendants while another hundred maidens dressed and adorned her.

What he ought to have spoken of was the poor Kurdish girl who owns nothing with which to cover her body or satisfy her hunger.

This came from the influence of Persian Sufism, with its ecstatic love and its aesthetics so close to the splendour of palaces and so distant from the suffering of the hungry.

Still, Khani did not entirely abandon the Sufi doctrine of poverty.

He wrote against inheritance, regarding the heir as someone who possesses wealth he did not labour to acquire. He called on the wealthy to spend their money on good works rather than pass it on as inheritance.

Whatever the case, I am not asking Ahmad Khani to travel centuries backward and become another al-Hallaj or al-Kilani.

He grew up in the age of Ottoman dervishism. When he tried to free himself from it, he turned to Persian Sufism and became one of the lovers.

What distinguished him was his national consciousness.

He raised the banner of revolt against those who had seized his country and enslaved his people.

He is therefore the father of the Kurdish revolution just as he is the father of Kurdish culture.

The Kurds owe him a debt greater than the crushing debts they continue to pay every day to their leaders.

A successful Arabic translation of Mem and Zin has been produced by the Kurdish disciple Jan Dost, son of Shaykh Mulla Bashir Shaykh Salih.

He introduced it with a short study of the author and the epic, and added notes explaining difficult meanings and symbols that show his strong command of the Sufi tradition.

Zin is pronounced with a clear z and an i-vowel.

Modern Sufi Pages

Tree

Adonis

Two stars fell.

Above the traveller’s head a cloud passed.

He bent down to receive the greeting.

A palm tree falls, and blood engraves its golden leaves.

A palm tree I taught to write.

It is an interpreter.

It is a notebook written in Arabic.

I taught it the Book

within the fence of hidden borders.

It is the beginning of place.

The winds are what remains.

I told you: Wake. I saw the water,

a child driving wind and stones.

And I said:

beneath the water and the fruit, beneath the skin of wheat,

a whisper dreams of becoming

a song for the wound

in the kingdom of hunger and tears.

Rise. I am calling you.

Have you known death?

I am your brother al-Khidr, the dowry of death.

I tear the door of time from its hinges.

I did not carry the wind. I did not hollow out a head.

In summer and in winter

I travel like a bird

down the river of hunger toward its enchanted mouth.

My kingdom wears the face of water.

I reign in absence.

I reign in wonder.

Awake or asleep,

it makes no difference whether you come near or move away.

My kingdom is in the light,

and the earth is the door of the house.

He called out, gathering the air,

carrying from every space a vein,

weaving for the West the robe of the East.

Jesus descends, bending over him,

green as the two stars.

He descends at the white minaret,

on the right-hand side of Damascus,

and kills Satan

on the right-hand side of Damascus.

And the darkness upon his road was shining.

It changed the names.

It loved the dead who would never return,

and abandoned the living.

The Star’s Insomnia — Exile

A poem by Abd al-Ilah al-Yasiri, a poet from Iraq.

A traveller on the path of steadfastness.

His conscience has four great preoccupations:

the state, colonialism, the turban, and the intellectuals.

He is an active fighter in our communalist field.

He supports taking over state palaces and hotels in order to house the poor.

Like Abd al-Qadir al-Jili, he believes that “the comfort of creation” is the root of everything.

He wants to take possession of Iraq so that he can distribute it among its hungry.

He lives by the work of his own hands.

Others drink from cups filled to the brim with wine.

My own cup holds labyrinths and grief.

Tired eyelids find their rest in sleep.

My eyes find rest in the company of stars.

If only my cares were like other people’s:

possessions, swords, money, office, profit.

My heart melts among them though they have hardened,

as a lamp melts in the depth of night.

I almost weep for them whenever they laugh.

I almost laugh at them whenever they mourn.

Against the wind, by some enchantment, without a compass,

I travel where there are no ships and no sailor.

Alone amid the uproar of night, forever silent:

when will I reach morning?

When will the night give way to dawn?

I am the stranger with a wound

that union with the beloved cannot quiet

and no surgeon can heal.

Today I received a card from him for the birthday of Jesus.

He wrote:

My sorrow and pain—not congratulations and not joy—on the birthday of our teacher, which the world celebrates by crucifying him all over again.

What can a grieving lover like me offer on this yearly catastrophe except flowers draped in black and steeped in tears?

His birth has been turned into an annual death of the spirit, an excuse for more profit in trade and more pleasure for the body.

Forgive my madness and the strange rhythm in which I move.

I have nothing to console me in what I am going through except my cup, which I drank to the voice of the Beloved.

I still drink from it.

I have not sobered from its wine, the wine that set me alight in this frozen world around me.

And while I was drunk, our teacher called to me and made me weep.

He said:

“What reward is there in loving someone who loves you?”

I answered:

“In him I have gathered all humanity, because he alone is still alive among these graves.”

Then he wept, and the light around me disappeared…

The Drunkard

Drunken one, grow still more awake through drunkenness.

Become alert.

Buy the cup with everything you own in this world,

and gain through it honour and splendour.

Discover in the wine the meaning within you that reason lost.

Reach the depth that revealed itself in you and reached its furthest point.

Sip from it

and see the light enthroned within you as God.

Erase from yourself every attribute,

every doubt and every confusion.

Merge into its spirit through love,

for you are nothing but that spirit.

Lose yourself in Him through Him:

in ecstasy, sorrow, and sighs.

You came to earth

so that silence might grow lips through you;

so that you might hold water inside stone for the trees;

so that you might clothe a bird in safety and in dreams.

Be nothing but what you choose to be,

in your own choosing and your own direction.

Prisoner of Water

Riyad al-Numani — an Iraqi communalist

Beneath the pearls of night in my master’s garden,

O father of the lily,

the daughter of light slept,

the third…

seven lilies in the blue.

All the gazelles of the earth gathered

to breathe her in,

rippling into perfume,

tracing tiny patterns from mysterious letters

with no dots upon them.

The rose tore open its clothes.

I broke every jar of wine.

Silence cried out.

Drunkenness surged.

The Absolute went mad.

My God…

save me.

I cannot bear cities.

You prolong Your coyness in me.

You turned abundance against me,

and I became like someone imprisoned

beneath a boat.

The Final Clause

By the Author

The morning stars disappear quickly before the face of the sun,

for the life of a star is limited.

And even to the one who is certain of the sun,

the life of the sun is limited.

In the Book of Certainties:

whoever seeks some possession on the earth will find it.

The deprived questioner is the one who asks about something and receives no answer.

Through negation he sees things.

Certainty is a sultan who sees heresy in negation.

And sultans, when you fail to understand them,

exile you.

So walk the roads of estrangement.

Do not submit to any depth.

Do not search for some distant end stored away in the Tablet, and do not write with any eyelid but your own.

Tablets have no memory.

There is no human being at the bottom.

The circle of the sky grows narrow when it is filled with anything other than thought: thought burning with the fire of ecstasy, kindled in the lands of care and intimate whispering.

Ecstasy contains hidden things that slip past all baggage.

The keeper of seals and power cannot see them.

Read them to him and he calls for the sword.

The poet, meanwhile, loses nothing of what he hopes for, because ecstasy is water mixed with fire.

With his eternal cup he fills the emptiness of every state.

It presses hard against the heart and forbids it everything other than the Beloved.

The heart says:

Sleep itself is an “other.”

So do not lose sight of the fire.

Your earthly heaven is adorned before you. The eye looks upon it and does not return humbled and defeated, as it recoils from a well suddenly blazing with flame.

If not, then let the walls fall.

The balance of things can be read.

There are mountains on the earth that do not sway with it.

Things themselves sway with the people who inhabit them.

Beginnings enchant the beating heart.

Yet at the beginning there is no human companion.

Fire begins from its end.

The root of the earth has no house in the belly of the earth where it can settle.

And you have no permanent resting place beneath the rule of the sun.

Abu Yazid, even beside the House, knows neither the Lord of the House nor the House itself.

For the Lord has lost His throne and His water in the wilderness.

He has entered evening in the deserts of bewilderment, without angels, a stranger within His own kingdoms, as though the earth had never come to Him willingly, the wind had never humbled itself before Him, and the ages had never submitted.

Return, questioner.

Thought is rebellion.

Thought has its stations, separated from one another by the Book of Poverty, moving from one day to the next in full wakefulness like al-Khawwas, without wings and without strings.

You are fertile seed in your sacred deprivation, and all creation is spread open before you.

From the spring of true existence comes the letter, climbing the peaks of the names.

The names are something hidden in the conscience of the universe.

The one who intends knows their essence when he holds fast to negation.

He walks through the hidden places of the letter tāʾ, full as the sand of the sea.

The laws deny him.

Action does not know him.

At the root of civilisations he has a voice that calls out to the people:

No wage belongs to the one who builds.

No deed belongs to the one who strives.

No rule belongs to the protected.

To conquer the ten thousand is humiliation.

Laws are like the morning star.

They do not understand the meaning of night.

Night is latency.

Those outside it do not know what night is:

there, separation is joined;

union is broken;

and the letter tāʾ stands at the heart of beginnings like water abandoned by the wind, all its sides becoming one.

In the deep sea are dimensions whose root the traveller circles in the suwayyira33 of absolute nothingness.

Do not ask about forms when they appear.

Do not ask when they flee.

Today you are insī—a human companion—and from the same root comes uns, intimacy.

You emerged naked from creation.

Thought is a wanderer.

Faith has shades of grey.

Will you be satisfied with merely being human?

Absolute nothingness surrounds the earth.

It is that thing without which the earth would not turn, the winds would not run across its shoulders, the sun would not pass over it, and you yourself would never have been.

The secret of the earth is before you like a lamp lit with its eastern oil.

Thought is rebellion.

You are beyond the summons of everything other than the Truth, beyond the voice that calls:

Be.

The passivity of things does not apply to your being.

Fire moves toward the sun as one equal moves toward another.

Fire has no equal but the sun.

Body, you who concern yourself with creation:

the time has come for the fire to consume you.

Through fire you will see the Truth without shadow.

Beyond distance there will be no further distance.

Dimensions will disappear.

Distances will dissolve.

And through fire, thought becomes rebellion.

If every human being is drowned beneath the wave of silence,

you will not drown…
